title: Building an Agent That Improves Its Own Harness
description: Turn repeated failures into tested changes, then use the evidence to improve the next experiment.
text: Imagine a coding agent encountering the same failure for the third time. A build produces thousands of lines of output. The useful diagnostic disappears from the model’s working context. The agent edits the wrong file, retries the build, and runs out of time. A developer adds another instruction: “Pay attention to compiler errors.” The next run still fails. The instruction asks the model to compensate for an information problem. The harness could preserve the complete log, surface the relevant diagnostics, and make the rest easy to inspect. That would change what the agent can actually work with. Now suppose the agent can propose that change, test it, and preserve it for future runs. Suppose it also remembers which experiments were useful and which apparently promising fixes caused regressions. We have the beginnings of a system that learns how to improve its own operation. The useful question is what an execution has earned the right to change. A single success might justify another experiment. A shared default needs evidence from other tasks. And an improvement to the search process needs its own test: does it make later improvements easier to find?

sections.title: Decide what should persist
sections.text: The harness is the software around a model: context construction, tool interfaces, state, recovery, and execution control. Harness learning can change those components while keeping the model’s weights fixed. The Self-Evolving Agent Harness paper makes persistence central to the definition: accepted revisions affect later runs, and an update mechanism remains available for further revisions. Its theoretical guarantees are conditional on assumptions such as independent validation; they do not make an arbitrary editing loop reliable. For implementation, distinguish three kinds of state. They have different purposes and need different evidence. State Compiler example Evidence needed Current task The build failed in a particular file The current execution record Reusable procedure A log reader preserves diagnostic spans and links to the full output Improvement on relevant fresh tasks, with regression checks Improvement experience Output filters should be tested on warning-dependent repairs Comparisons showing what the earlier filter preserved and lost A retry can repair the current task without changing future behavior. A procedure can help future tasks without teaching the optimizer anything. Improvement experience changes which patches and tests the optimizer considers next. This extends the question in The Quality Flywheel : what useful knowledge survives the experiment? Here, some of that knowledge concerns how to run the next experiment.

sections.title: Locate the change
sections.text: Several approaches can improve an agent while keeping model weights fixed. The distinction is what they retain and where that retained material acts. Approach What persists What it changes next Prompt optimization, as in GEPA’s original paper Selected prompt variants informed by execution feedback Instructions used by the application Reflection memory, as in Reflexion Verbal lessons from earlier attempts Decisions in subsequent trials Code evolution, as in the Darwin Gödel Machine An archive of modified agent implementations Tools and execution logic, including code used for further modification Improvement experience, as in Harness² Reusable harnesses and lessons about their refinement Which adaptations the improver proposes and composes These categories overlap: prompts belong to harnesses, and lessons can guide code edits. GEPA’s current implementation also supports code and configuration; the table refers to its original prompt study. Better task results support a better agent. Better subsequent search under a matched budget supports a better improver. Harness² connects task-local adaptation with an accumulating improvement library. Each new task starts from a common base harness; earlier components and lessons guide its adaptation. Model weights, stage instructions, and the decision rule remain fixed. On WorkBuddy-Bench, Gemini 3.5 Flash under OpenCode improves from 72.4 to 77.5 with one improvement step; removing the library reduces that result to 74.4. This supports a contribution from accumulated experience, without establishing indefinite acceleration. Harmony Harness tackles competing objectives through functionality and security evaluation, modular changes, and scope-aware composition. Its results motivate checking what an average conceals. Its small evaluation splits—30 tasks each for SecRepoBench and 28 for BaxBench—and narrow observed trade-off frontier also limit the conclusions.

sections.title: Choose where improvement happens
sections.text: Harness² adapts around the task currently being solved, using execution contrasts when a reliable verifier is unavailable. The design below instead searches offline and uses trusted tests to admit shared versions. This is a deployment choice, not a reproduction of that paper. Decision Adapt during a task Search offline for a shared version Feedback Current task traces and output comparisons A development workload with outcome checks Latency Proposals and probes add to that task’s wait Search runs separately from requests Side effects Probes need isolated copies or reversible actions Resettable environments support repeated comparisons Cost Adaptation must justify its cost on that request Search cost can be spread over later uses Persistence Keep local facts and provisional adaptations local Promote a scoped change only after fresh validation For the compiler example, start offline: build output is reproducible, functional tests exist, and the failure recurs. A successful adaptation for one repository can enter the candidate pool, but it needs broader evidence before becoming a default. Development evidence changes the next proposal. Fresh promotion checks and a limited rollout decide what ships; the protected audit assesses the frozen process. Development results feed the improver. The audit stays outside that feedback loop. If a promotion failure is later opened for diagnosis, mark those cases as exposed and validate the revision on fresh cases.

sections.title: Turn the failure into a patch hypothesis
sections.text: Start with the trace. Did the tool return the diagnostic? Did an output limit remove it? Did compaction discard it later? Did the model see it and misunderstand it? Each explanation points to a different component. A prompt cannot recover evidence that never reaches the model. Write a hypothesis that can fail: “On long build outputs, preserving structured diagnostic spans will increase repair success because the agent can inspect the first relevant failure without losing access to the complete log.” The candidate might modify a tool wrapper. It saves the original output in a task-scoped artifact, extracts diagnostics with locations, and returns a compact receipt. The complete log remains accessible under the same task permissions. An illustrative interface could return: { "exit_code": 1, "full_output": "artifacts/build-17.log", "diagnostics": "artifacts/build-17.diagnostics.json", "preview": "src/parser.cc:148: incompatible return type", "preview_complete": false, "extraction_status": "partial" } These fields describe different facts. A complete raw log does not imply complete extraction. A short preview does not imply there is only one error. If extraction fails, the receipt must expose that failure and point to the raw output. This builds on progressive disclosure for agent tools : keep large evidence available, and make the next useful read easy to discover. Keep the first patch small enough to diagnose. For this experiment, change only the output adapter. Hold prompts, model, and retrieval policy fixed. Coordinated edits can come later, with comparisons that establish why the combination helps.

sections.title: Give the improver a search procedure
sections.text: The improver can be the same generalist model, running in an isolated workspace. It needs a bounded editing task, relevant evidence, and an explicit selection rule. Freeze the current production version, the incumbent , for one search cycle. Choose a recurring failure family by frequency and impact. Retrieve lessons that match its symptoms, component, and toolchain, including failed attempts. Require the proposer to return a hypothesis, applicability conditions, a patch, and a predicted regression to check. Here is pseudocode for a deliberately small search. All candidates branch from the same incumbent; a rejected patch can inform a later proposal without entering production. base, library = snapshot(incumbent, experience) budget = search_budget_after_reserving_final_checks() journal, candidates = [], [] while budget.can_start_attempt() and not stop_rule(journal): failure = choose_failure(development_traces, journal) lessons = retrieve(library, journal, failure) proposal = propose(base, failure, lessons, editable_files) candidate = apply_in_isolated_workspace(base, proposal.patch) checks = validate(candidate, allowed_diff, schemas, smoke_tests) if not checks.pass: journal.append(proposal, checks) continue report = compare_on_reset_tasks( base, candidate, development_tasks, protocol ) journal.append(proposal, report) if protocol.development_eligible(report): candidates.append(candidate, report) freeze(journal) candidate = select_by_declared_rule(candidates) return candidate, journal # No candidate means keep the incumbent. For example, allow at most eight proposals and stop after three attempts without improving the best eligible development score. A separate time and token cap covers every attempt, including invalid patches and retrieval; reserve budget for the final checks. These are starting settings, not research-derived constants. Validate the actual diff against the allowed files, check that the receipt schema still parses, and run focused contract and smoke tests. The proposer’s description of what it changed is insufficient. Keep evaluator code, hidden tasks, permissions, and release controls outside the candidate workspace. Declare selection before searching: require the minimum development gain and all regression and cost limits, then rank eligible candidates by task score. Break ties by lower execution cost, then smaller patch size. This simple policy may miss useful combinations. It makes the first implementation inspectable; an archive or broader search can be added when that limitation becomes measurable. Comparisons need identical starting repositories, inputs, tool versions, and resource limits. Reset between attempts and randomize run order to reduce time-dependent bias. Recorded responses cannot substitute for a resettable environment when a new policy takes different actions. Use trusted outcome tests; candidate-generated tests can diagnose a defect but cannot independently validate the candidate. Each journal entry records the parent version, patch, library snapshot, model, environment, task IDs, traces, outcomes, and total cost. Failed attempts remain available to the next proposal. The selected candidate goes to a separate promotion evaluator.

sections.title: Let the first candidate fail
sections.text: Suppose generation one produces an error-only output filter. Evaluate it on 120 development tasks, with five runs per task. The following numbers are invented to illustrate the decision; no implementation was measured. Each family contains 40 tasks, giving 200 runs per family for each harness. A family is a task slice: a subset with a shared property worth checking. Task family Incumbent passes First candidate passes Change in pass rate Large error logs 100 / 200 160 / 200 +30 percentage points Small error logs 150 / 200 160 / 200 +5 percentage points Repairs requiring warnings 140 / 200 118 / 200 −11 percentage points All tasks 390 / 600 438 / 600 +8 percentage points The aggregate improves from 65% to 73%, but warning-dependent repairs get worse. If the declared limit permits at most a two-point decline in an important slice, this candidate is ineligible. A useful idea has produced an unacceptable default. Inspect the failing traces before assigning a cause. The filter may have removed a useful warning, but run variability or another adapter bug could also explain failures. The measurement is evidence of a regression; warning loss is a hypothesis to test. Calculate each task’s average score across repetitions, subtract its incumbent average, and average those differences: task gain = mean(candidate runs) − mean(incumbent runs) overall gain = mean(task gains) Repetitions expose execution variability. They do not turn 120 distinct tasks into 600 independent task examples. Estimate uncertainty with a method that preserves task grouping, such as resampling tasks with all their runs together. If repositories or task templates introduce further dependence, preserve that grouping too. Set the primary outcome, slices, acceptable regressions, and comparison budget in advance. Use declared workload weights if the task mix differs from deployment traffic. Development scores guide search; fresh promotion evidence must resolve uncertainty before release.

sections.title: Make the second proposal remember the first
sections.text: The useful lesson is more specific than “shorter output is better.” Store the measured regression separately from its suspected cause. # Hypothetical development record, not a framework schema. trigger: long compiler output obscures actionable diagnostics change: error-only diagnostic preview with raw-log access observation: warning-dependent pass rate fell by 11 points hypothesis: required warnings were omitted from the preview next_check: trace whether omitted warnings explain failed repairs scope: tested compiler versions and output formats status: rejected_for_release provenance: [parent_version, patch_id, task_ids, trace_ids, results] Generation two starts from the unchanged incumbent. Its retrieval step finds this record before proposing another filter. The improver examines a failing trace and checks whether the relevant warning existed in the raw log, disappeared from the preview, and was never fetched. A controlled comparison that restores that warning can test the proposed mechanism. It now proposes an adapter that preserves errors, warnings, and attached diagnostic notes with their locations. The preview has a size limit; a structured index makes omitted diagnostics discoverable. The receipt distinguishes a truncated preview from incomplete extraction, and raw-log access remains available when parsing fails. The earlier failure also changes the tests chosen before the expensive task runs: Case added to development checks Contract to verify Warning appears before the first error Warning remains in the index and can be retrieved Diagnostic spans several lines Location, message, and attached notes stay together Toolchain output is unrecognized Extraction reports uncertainty and exposes the raw log Preview exceeds its limit Receipt marks truncation and points to remaining diagnostics These checks test the adapter’s behavior. The next paired task comparison tests whether the agent actually uses that behavior to repair programs. Keeping a warning available does not ensure the model reads it. This completes the second proposal, not a fictional success story: the new candidate still needs measurements. It can improve, tie, or regress again. The recursive step is already visible—the first experiment changed both the next patch and the next test plan. Version the experience library separately from the execution harness. Freeze the historical library for each search cycle and retain that cycle’s development journal. Consolidate duplicate lessons, preserve counterevidence, and revalidate stale entries after model or tool changes. Keep task artifacts and retrieved lessons within their original access boundaries.

sections.title: Promote the version that survives new evidence
sections.text: Freeze the selected patch and its applicability rule. Run it against the incumbent on fresh promotion tasks, using the outcome, uncertainty method, slice limits, and resource budgets declared before search. For example, require the lower confidence bound on overall gain to exceed a chosen minimum, while the uncertainty bounds for important slices rule out a loss larger than the allowed decline. Choose the error rate and comparison budget together; repeatedly testing candidates until one passes defeats the check. Use historical failures as a regression suite alongside fresh tasks. Separate related repositories and near-duplicate tasks across partitions where possible. Route a specialized adapter using information available before execution, such as compiler identity and supported output format. A rule that depends on knowing whether a task will pass is unusable. A passing candidate enters a canary , a limited rollout with predefined success and rollback criteria. Record the harness version on every run. If the rollout passes, update the production version pointer; otherwise restore the incumbent. Rollback affects future runs and cannot undo external writes, so action-taking workflows need isolated probes before live exposure. An audit evaluates the frozen selection process on a further untouched set. If its outcomes change the design, that set has become development evidence and a later claim needs fresh audit data. Record rejected searches as well as releases; reporting only successful searches conceals the cost and failure rate. For our example, the release record would connect the second adapter to its development report, fresh promotion report, applicability rule, canary decision, and rollback target. Until those reports exist, it remains a candidate.

sections.title: Test whether the improver improved
sections.text: A better deployed harness establishes one result. A better improver requires another experiment. Start each condition from the same base harness, proposer model, development tasks, and total search budget. Use only experience from earlier, separate tasks: Condition Available history What the comparison tests A No accumulated library Search without prior components or lessons B Earlier components and their applicability metadata Value of reusable implementations C The same components plus experiment lessons and counterevidence Additional value of learning how to improve Keep retrieval limits and accounting consistent. Run multiple search trials, then evaluate frozen selections on unseen tasks with the same protocol. Compare C with B to estimate the added value of experiment lessons, rather than attributing inherited code to a better search process. Compare B with A to estimate component reuse. These are controlled comparisons, not guarantees of transfer. Measure final task quality, regressions, total search cost, and the number of proposals needed to reach a predefined target. Include searches that never reach it; report their spent budget and failure to qualify. Additional attempts with the original harness and a static curated skill are useful simpler baselines under the same total budget. Count proposal, probe, judging, retrieval, and memory-maintenance costs. An offline search costing 60 units and saving 0.2 units per later task breaks even after 300 tasks, assuming equal quality and no additional maintenance cost. That illustrative calculation fails if the change expires before 300 uses, or its quality loss outweighs the savings. Repeat across fresh batches and after distribution changes. Task-order seeds do not necessarily control model sampling; Harness²’s experiment guide makes that distinction explicit. Record both. When gains flatten, revisit the search space, retrieval, and workload. Another recursive round may not help.

sections.title: Build the smallest loop that can earn a release
sections.text: Build one loop around one recurring failure family. The first useful milestone is a complete, inspectable chain: a trace, a proposed patch, a failed comparison, a lesson that changes the next proposal, and a candidate that survives fresh evaluation. The implementation can consist of a trace store, a versioned candidate workspace, a runner that resets task environments, an evaluator, an experience index, and a release pointer. It does not require permanent specialist agents. As argued in Before You Build Another Agent , keep expertise reusable and delegate bounded work when separate execution earns its cost. Choose components you actually control. If an underlying SDK owns compaction and its internal execution loop, begin with exposed context files, tool wrappers, skills, or supported hooks. A proposal to edit inaccessible internals is not an executable improvement. Expand the editable surface only when the existing loop finds useful gains and catches meaningful regressions. If the improver later proposes changing its own retrieval or proposal policy, evaluate that policy against the previous one from a common base with matched search budgets. Keep the external promotion standard fixed. The next time the compiler failure appears, the agent should inherit a better way to inspect the evidence. The next time the optimizer proposes an output filter, it should inherit the warning regression and the test that caught it. That is a concrete form of progress: both the work and the method for improving the work have learned from the failure.

sections.title: Run the warning-preservation experiment
sections.text: The engineering workbench contains four fixed build transcripts and explicit required diagnostics. Run python workbench.py to compare raw output, errors-only output, and errors-plus-warnings. Inspect adapter-cases.json before the report: a warning-only regression is the case that the aggressive filter hides. The companion also includes compiler_experiment.py , which compiles and executes three Java programs in three trials each. On OpenJDK 17.0.20, the unchecked-cast case compiled successfully with a 216-byte warning and failed at runtime in all three trials. The errors-only adapter discarded the warning completely. Inspect compiler-results.json for the raw diagnostics, exit codes, and environment. This is a narrow compiler experiment, not an agent benchmark. The report records retained requirements and UTF-8 bytes; bytes are not tokens or model cost. The conservative adapter passes these four cases, but a diagnostic with an unfamiliar prefix can still defeat it. Add that case before extending the rule. For a real harness experiment, freeze model, tool versions, task IDs, and budgets; store every raw response alongside the transformed view. Run the baseline and candidate on the same held-out tasks, report repeated trials and latency, and keep promotion outside the optimizer. A smaller response is useful only if downstream completion and authority checks survive.

title: How to Write and Score an Agent Eval
description: From a plausible wrong answer to a defensible release decision: nine chapters on writing tests, calculating scores, and checking whether success repeats.
text: A correct diagnosis can still produce an unsafe recommendation. This guide uses an illustrative checkout incident to separate those judgments, turn them into a scoring contract, and decide what a release result actually supports. Three parts contain nine chapters. Each part can be read on its own: Design the Test : define the task, evidence, valid alternatives, and rubric. Build the Score : inspect correctness, completion, authority, and the interactive scoring example. Trust the Result : calibrate judgments, account for repeated runs, and assess a release. Download the Python scoring companion and the paired-comparison workbench . The supplied judgments and datasets are illustrative. They are not measured model results. Inside this collection

sections.text: Reproduce the failure, establish the evidence, and write rubrics that accept valid alternatives while rejecting plausible mistakes. 7 min read ↗ 02

sections.text: Turn one execution into verifiable judgments. Separate correctness, grounding, permissions, and completion—then calculate each score. 10 min read ↗ 03

sections.text: Handle missing judgments, calibrate graders, repeat trials, and make a release decision that the headline score can justify. 12 min read ↗

title: Implementing Progressive Disclosure for Agent Tools
description: Build one discoverable CLI for MCP, SQL, and REST, with precise schemas, scoped execution, and honest result receipts.
text: An agent is asked which production services are still running a faulty release. The answer requires deployment inventory, service ownership, and perhaps logs. The agent already has a sandbox and can write code. What it needs is a practical way to discover the available interfaces and use them without loading their entire documentation into context. A large tool catalog supplied upfront makes every task pay for capabilities it may never use. A single generic executor can hide that catalog, but the agent still needs to learn what it can execute. Make discovery explicit, execution composable, and results selectively readable. In The World an Agent Can Read , I described how small indexes make a knowledge collection navigable. We can apply the same structure to APIs, database schemas, and tool servers. Here is a concrete design using a shared CLI called toolbox . The commands are proposed interfaces; a runnable fixture below checks the SQL and result contracts against synthetic data.

sections.title: Start with a small entry point
sections.text: The harness gives the agent a short index of the connections available to this task. Each entry describes the questions the connection can answer and points to its documentation. # Available connections - observability: Search runtime logs by service, release, and time window. Read connections/observability.md for MCP discovery and invocation. - production: Query observed runtime instances and service ownership. Read connections/production.md for SQL schema discovery and query usage. - incidents: Find existing incidents for a service or release. Read connections/incidents.md for REST operations and pagination. The connection documents explain MCP invocation, SQL views, and REST operations. Generate the index from the task's configured connections: the model sees routing descriptions and can retrieve detailed contracts when needed. The same three operations guide each adapter: list what is available, describe a selected capability, and execute it. We can implement that pattern for MCP, SQL, and REST. The CLI can fetch, index, and cache metadata without printing it all. Only selected output reaches the model. A catalog stored in a file remains working data; repeatedly inserting it into model requests consumes context.

sections.title: Start with MCP tools
sections.text: Suppose the observability server publishes a query_logs tool. The agent can discover its contract and use it when the investigation calls for logs: toolbox mcp observability list-tools toolbox mcp observability describe query_logs toolbox mcp observability call query_logs \ --json-file log-query.json \ --output logs.json A compact list-tools response might be: { "tools": [{"name":"query_logs","summary":"Search runtime logs"}], "next_cursor": null } describe query_logs expands that selected entry into the invocation contract: { "name": "query_logs", "inputSchema": { "type": "object", "properties": { "service_id": {"type":"string"}, "release_id": {"type":"string"}, "start": {"type":"string","format":"date-time"}, "end": {"type":"string","format":"date-time"} }, "required": ["service_id","release_id","start","end"], "additionalProperties": false } } The agent can create log-query.json with those four fields. The adapter validates inputs and checks structured outputs against any published output schema. The compact listing is a CLI presentation of the full catalog held by the adapter. The adapter contract should make the MCP protocol mapping explicit: CLI behavior Adapter behavior list-tools Follow tools/list cursors, cache definitions, and expose a compact, paginated index describe <name> Read the selected catalog entry; this is a CLI operation, not a separate MCP method call <name> Validate arguments and send tools/call ; map both JSON-RPC errors and isError: true results to nonzero CLI exits Save a result Preserve MCP content and structuredContent ; do not force every response into SQL rows Tool-result pagination belongs to the application schema; catalog pagination does not solve it. A generic adapter can save one response completely while leaving the application's next-page token untouched. It must distinguish those facts. list-tools exposes only published tools. If a server publishes one code executor, the CLI cannot turn its internal functions into separate tools. The adapter standardizes access to existing capabilities.

sections.title: Then discover and query SQL
sections.text: To find affected services, the production connection exposes a query service and schema metadata. A generic execute_sql entry point alone would still leave the agent guessing which tables mean what. Give it discovery commands: toolbox sql production list-tables toolbox sql production describe inventory_snapshots toolbox sql production describe runtime_instances toolbox sql production describe services list-tables returns names and short descriptions, with pagination when necessary. describe returns the complete contract for one selected view. For a large catalog, add a search entry point: toolbox sql production search-schema \ "currently running releases and service owners"

sections.title: Make the schema useful enough to write the query
sections.text: The distinction between rollout history and observed runtime state matters in this investigation. A deployment event can record an attempted release that was later rolled back. The agent needs a view of observed instances. A useful schema describes types, nullability, keys, and what each row means. This excerpt captures the domain details: { "view": "runtime_instances", "row_meaning": "One observed instance in one inventory snapshot", "unique_key": ["snapshot_id", "instance_id"], "columns": { "snapshot_id": "Inventory capture identifier", "instance_id": "Observed runtime instance", "service_id": "Joins to services.service_id", "environment": "prod, staging, or dev", "release_id": "Release observed on this instance" }, "coverage": "Read the selected snapshot's capture metadata" } The services description establishes a unique, non-null service_id and exposes name and owner_team from the current service directory. Runtime service IDs are also non-null, but matching directory entries can be absent. Structural catalogs such as INFORMATION_SCHEMA supply columns and types; maintained descriptions supply domain meaning.

sections.title: Find the snapshot before using it
sections.text: In this connection, inventory_snapshots describes immutable captures. Its contract says that finished means collection has stopped; coverage is reported separately. The following query selects the latest finished production capture: SELECT snapshot_id, observed_at, scope, coverage_complete, missing_regions FROM inventory_snapshots WHERE environment = :environment AND capture_status = 'finished' ORDER BY observed_at DESC, snapshot_id DESC LIMIT 1; Save this as snapshot.sql ; scope.json contains {"environment":"prod"} . Run the query and inspect the selected row: toolbox sql production query \ --file snapshot.sql --params-file scope.json --output snapshot.json jq '.rows[0]' snapshot.json { "snapshot_id": "snapshot-184", "observed_at": "2026-10-18T02:00:00Z", "scope": "authorized production inventory", "coverage_complete": false, "missing_regions": ["region-c"] } The adapter normalizes database JSON and boolean values into these JSON types. If no finished capture exists, report that gap. If its observation time is too old for the question, refresh through the supported inventory operation or state the limitation. The latest available capture is not necessarily fresh enough. The agent now has a snapshot ID and its limitations. Each captured instance appears once, so counting rows counts observed instances on the faulty release. Use a left join to retain affected services whose ownership metadata is missing: SELECT i.service_id, s.name, s.owner_team, COUNT(*) AS affected_instances FROM runtime_instances AS i LEFT JOIN services AS s ON s.service_id = i.service_id WHERE i.snapshot_id = :snapshot_id AND i.environment = :environment AND i.release_id = :release_id GROUP BY i.service_id, s.name, s.owner_team ORDER BY affected_instances DESC, i.service_id; Save the query as affected.sql . Put the user-selected values in parameters.json ; the SQL adapter binds them as values rather than substituting them into the SQL string. In this connection, snapshot_id is reserved for the execution context selected with --snapshot . The adapter translates the placeholder notation for its database driver. { "environment": "prod", "release_id": "R42" } toolbox sql production query \ --snapshot snapshot-184 \ --file affected.sql --params-file parameters.json \ --output affected.json

sections.title: Attach provenance where the read is enforced
sections.text: --snapshot is a documented capability of the production connection. Its query service opens an authorized, immutable capture and exposes that capture's runtime instances alongside the authorized current service directory. Runtime queries require this context. The service binds snapshot_id , rejects parameter overrides, and attaches capture metadata to its response. The CLI copies it into the receipt. Coverage describes the runtime capture; current directory entries may still be missing. At the service boundary: capture = inventory.open_authorized_snapshot(user, request.snapshot_id) catalog = readonly_catalog(capture.instances, authorized_directory(user)) params = bind_reserved(request.params, snapshot_id=capture.id) rows = catalog.query(request.sql, params, budget=request_budget) return rows, capture.metadata Snapshot files or restricted views can implement the catalog. The guarantee is that runtime inventory reads cannot escape the selected capture. Generic SQL connections without backend provenance report unknown coverage. Backend budgets still bound query work.

sections.title: Give large results somewhere to live
sections.text: Saving to a file must also change what the harness sends back to the model. A CLI that writes the file and then prints its entire contents has gained little. In the proposed contract, --output writes the data and prints a small receipt. Here is an illustrative receipt for the SQL query: { "execution": "succeeded", "result": { "path": "affected.json", "row_count": 2, "complete": true }, "source": { "snapshot_id": "snapshot-184", "observed_at": "2026-10-18T02:00:00Z", "scope": "authorized production inventory", "coverage_complete": false, "missing_regions": ["region-c"] } } Here, result.complete means every row returned by the requested SQL query was saved. It says nothing about missing source regions. source.coverage_complete is true only with supporting backend metadata, false for known gaps, and null when unknown. MCP receipts should likewise name what was retrieved—a single response or an application-defined full export—before claiming completion. The SQL result file uses a rows envelope. Inspecting it gives the two affected services: jq '.rows[:5]' affected.json [ {"service_id":"svc-payments","name":"payments", "owner_team":"commerce","affected_instances":3}, {"service_id":"svc-unknown","name":null, "owner_team":null,"affected_instances":1} ] The answer can now be precise: “At 02:00 UTC, the captured inventory shows three R42 instances in payments and one in svc-unknown. Ownership is unavailable for svc-unknown. Region-c was not covered, so this does not establish the full production impact.” The missing owner remains visible instead of removing the affected service from the answer. A local Python or JavaScript program can aggregate larger datasets, join results, or select evidence. The harness returns its chosen output. This separation between accessible data and model context is developed in Local Context for Autonomous Agents .

sections.title: Extend the same interface to REST
sections.text: Suppose the investigation also needs existing incidents for an affected service. A REST adapter can expose approved operations from an OpenAPI description , or a maintained catalog when the API has no usable specification. toolbox rest incidents list-operations toolbox rest incidents describe listIncidents toolbox rest incidents call listIncidents \ --json-file incident-query.json --output incidents.json list-operations returns names and summaries. describe expands one operation into its method, path, parameter locations, response contract, and authorization requirements. In this illustrative catalog, listIncidents maps to GET /incidents and accepts service_id , release_id , and state as query parameters. The corresponding incident-query.json is: { "query": { "service_id": "svc-payments", "release_id": "R42", "state": "open" } } The adapter validates the envelope, encodes the parameters according to the operation contract, and calls the configured service through the trusted gateway. Path parameters and request bodies use separate envelope fields when required. The agent selects a documented operation; the connection controls the destination and credentials. Pagination needs a connection-specific contract. If this API returns next_cursor , the adapter must either follow its documented cursor mapping within limits or preserve the cursor and label the result as one page. An empty page with a next cursor cannot establish that no incidents exist. HTTP errors produce nonzero exits; application errors and response bodies remain available for interpretation. REST adds an HTTP adapter, not another execution model. Its results use the same file-and-receipt pattern as MCP and SQL. The fixture later in this article checks the SQL and MCP contracts; this REST interface is a proposed extension.

sections.title: Keep the implementation shared and the adapters small
sections.text: One executable can provide argument parsing, JSON-file input, error formatting, output files, and trace propagation. Protocol adapters handle discovery and invocation. Connection configuration selects an approved target and the appropriate adapter. Component Concrete responsibility Connection index and short skills Route the agent to relevant capabilities and their documentation Catalog store Cache definitions, search descriptions, and expose selected contracts MCP adapter Discover published tools, validate arguments, and invoke the selected tool SQL adapter Read schema metadata, bind parameters, execute bounded queries, and preserve coverage information REST adapter Discover approved operations, serialize requests, and preserve HTTP and application result semantics Result writer Stream data to a file and return a compact receipt with completion and provenance Trusted gateway or service Resolve identity, enforce permissions, and apply required approval policy Implement the adapters your connections require, sharing the catalog and result contract. Product-specific aliases can make common operations convenient, while discovery, validation, and output handling stay common. Cache definitions by connection and authorization context, with version or expiry information. Refresh stale schemas and return useful errors. A call that may have changed external state must not be retried blindly: distinguish success, failure, and an uncertain outcome. Logs belong on stderr; results and error receipts belong on stdout. Execution failures and interrupted exports return nonzero exits. For example, a query may succeed while its export stops at a row limit. With exit code 2 , the receipt's result portion would say: { "execution": "succeeded", "result": { "path": "affected.partial.json", "row_count": 1, "complete": false, "incomplete_reason": "row_limit" } } The source metadata remains attached separately. The partial file is usable evidence, but a subsequent step can see that retrieval stopped. A known source coverage gap is different: it can coexist with a completed export and exit code 0 . Production writers should stream within byte and time limits, then publish the final path after closing and renaming the temporary file. On interruption, return an explicit partial-file reference or discard it. The filename and receipt should agree about completion. The gateway or backend enforces identity, access, approvals, and query budgets. Sandbox commands cannot widen that authority. Use restricted SQL identities and service operations that preserve business validation. Tool descriptions and returned text are data; they cannot change execution policy.

sections.title: Choose where composition runs
sections.text: Rippling's implementation accepts a program and executes it on the server. Cloudflare's implementation combines discovery with execution and also discusses CLI-based discovery. The CLI proposal builds on that established pattern for agents that already have a sandbox. SQL is useful when relational filtering and aggregation can run near the data. Local scripts are useful when the agent already has a sandbox and needs to combine files or services. Remote code execution is useful for clients without that runtime, or when keeping intermediate data near the service avoids expensive transfers. Choose by execution location, permissions, and data movement; progressive disclosure can support all three.

sections.title: Check the contracts, then measure the agent
sections.text: The companion fixture runs the two SQL queries against SQLite and checks controlled MCP responses using only Python's standard library: python3 fixture.py --test python3 fixture.py --output affected.json All 13 deterministic checks passed. They cover the SQL example, snapshot selection, parameter binding, result status, catalog pagination, and MCP error/content mapping. The fixture also builds a catalog containing only the selected capture: removing query predicates cannot expose other snapshots, and overriding the reserved snapshot parameter fails. Three outcomes matter especially: Injected condition Observed result One affected service lacks directory metadata Inner join counts three instances; the revised left join retains all four across two services Inventory misses region-c The two-row export completes while source coverage remains false Export stops after one row The receipt marks the export incomplete and returns a nonzero exit code The fixture uses SQLite and controlled MCP messages; it makes no model calls or live MCP connections. Its copied catalog demonstrates data scope, not a security boundary for hostile SQL. The writer materializes rows; authentication, streaming, and schema validation remain production work. These checks establish the illustrated contracts, not improved agent success or token cost. Evaluate agent behavior separately with three explicit conditions: the full catalog supplied upfront; a short index with deferred discovery; and an oracle condition supplying only the relevant definitions. Keep the model, task, data, permissions, output handling, and execution options fixed. Otherwise a change in result handling could be mistaken for a discovery improvement. Across repeated tasks, score affected-service identification, observation time, and coverage qualification separately. Include missing metadata, an incomplete capture, a schema change, and a partial export. An interrupted result must not turn into a confident “nothing is affected.” Record task success, total input and output tokens across all turns, discovery calls, elapsed time, and backend work. Report variation across runs rather than one favorable trace. The oracle condition helps distinguish a discovery failure from a reasoning failure after the relevant contract is available. The Next Useful Question offers the corresponding test for each retrieval: does the evidence change what the agent can decide? The CLI earns its complexity only if those complete tasks improve. One shared CLI, small protocol adapters, a discoverable catalog, and an explicit result contract are enough to start. The agent can find a tool, query a snapshot, inspect an API operation, and explain what the evidence covers. Those small interfaces determine whether progressive disclosure produces a reliable answer.

sections.title: A first adapter you can actually finish
sections.text: Start with the downloadable fixture’s SQL snapshot and expected coverage, then expose a single read-only MCP operation that returns the same receipt. Confirm that protocol errors and tool-level isError results remain distinct, and compare the transport output with the fixture before adding REST. The ZIP provides controlled SQL/MCP examples; it does not ship the proposed toolbox CLI or a production transport. Record a transcript with discovery query, selected schema version, exact call, raw result, export-complete flag, expected scope, and missing scope. An exhausted cursor can coexist with missing owners. In the engineering workbench , evidence_complete deliberately returns false when only one of those conditions holds. To test disclosure quality, compare full catalogue, deferred catalogue, and an oracle-selected interface under the same task, model, tool results, and budget. Count failed discovery and abandoned tasks as outcomes. Until those runs exist, context savings are a hypothesis rather than evidence of better agent performance.

title: Before you build another agent
description: Build a strong generalist. Make expertise discoverable. Delegate only when the task earns it.
text: “Our application became slow after the release.” A smaller connection pool can trigger queueing, retries, and more load. A deployment agent, a database agent, and a networking agent might each identify a symptom. The diagnosis depends on connecting them. For an assistant that works across products, build one capable generalist as the primary agent. Give it a harness that progressively exposes the knowledge and tools it needs. Permit additional agents only as temporary, dynamically delegated subagents with enforced limits. Permanent specialists are separately routed agents with fixed domain roles. Stable, repetitive workloads can make that routing attractive: context and latency are easier to tune. For a cross-product assistant, however, routing, context transfer, and reconciliation also create opportunities for coordination failures . A specialist label adds no capability by itself. Preserve distinct capabilities through model selection, authorized tools, and scoped domain memory.

sections.title: Keep the investigation coherent
sections.text: The generalist needs durable task state : the objective, evidence, hypotheses, and open questions. Preserve it across compaction and restarts, with links to source artifacts. This lets the agent connect a deployment change to database behavior several steps later. The investigation crosses domains while the primary agent retains the evidence and responsibility for the answer. The harness is the runtime around the model: context management, tool discovery, code execution, permissions, and recovery. Build these capabilities once and reuse them across tasks.

sections.title: Make expertise discoverable
sections.text: Progressive disclosure gives the agent broad reach with focused context. Start with a compact knowledge index and tool catalog. Retrieve relevant documents , discover tool schemas on demand , and load procedures as needed. The generalist can follow the investigation from deployments to databases while retaining its context. Package expertise as reusable skills : diagnostic principles, procedures, examples, and scripts. Filter large tool results in code before adding them to context. Product teams contribute knowledge, tools, and evaluations to the shared harness. Discovery is a capability to test. SkillsBench found that curated skills improved average pass rates, while some tasks regressed. A study of realistic skill retrieval found that gains weakened when agents had to find and select relevant skills. Test the path from symptom to useful context to correct tool use; preload essentials when latency matters. If supplying the right material fixes a failure, improve discovery. If it does not, investigate the model, tool, or procedure before adding agent boundaries.

sections.title: Allow only bounded dynamic delegation
sections.text: A subagent is a temporary execution created through the primary agent’s delegation tool. Require three things: a separable question, a reason for separate execution—parallel progress, context isolation, or independent review—and a result the primary agent can verify without repeating the investigation . Simple lookups and predictable procedures belong in tools, scripts, or deterministic workflows . Dynamic-only delegation is the policy proposed here. The evidence supports choosing by task structure: a controlled study of 260 configurations across six benchmarks , with matched compute budgets, found gains on decomposable financial tasks and losses on sequential planning tasks. Anthropic’s research system demonstrates parallel research followed by synthesis. Its reported gains also involved different models and more compute. Neither result establishes that dynamic delegation is universally best. The primary agent proposes the work; the runtime enforces the limits: Limit Runtime enforcement Purpose Creation Primary agent only; require a current-task contract Keep spawning under one owner Lifetime Create a task-scoped execution; end it on completion, timeout, or parent termination Keep delegation temporary Fan-out Cap concurrent executions and total launches, including retries Prevent unbounded spawning Depth Subagents cannot delegate further Prevent recursive expansion Resources Reserve from the parent budget; cap time and tool calls Bound total task cost Access Restrict data and tools to the parent’s authority Prevent privilege expansion Do not install routes that automatically send database questions to a database agent. Templates can supply instructions; delegation must be chosen for the current task. Subagents use the same harness with isolated state. Depth one gives up nested delegation to keep ownership and budget accounting simple. Mandatory checks and approvals belong in runtime policy or deterministic workflows. If delegation is denied, continue directly, narrow the task, or escalate within the same limits.

sections.title: Delegate a question you can verify
sections.text: In the latency investigation, the generalist can trace request flow while a subagent asks: “Did this release change connection pool behavior?” Its contract includes the deployment diff, telemetry, documentation, and read-only tools. The result must include findings, source evidence, counterevidence, uncertainty, and completion status. Suppose the diff shows a pool limit falling from 100 to 20. That establishes a change, not its causal role. The generalist checks whether connection wait time rose with the release and proposes a controlled test. Evidence that does not fit stays visible. A separate review can challenge this explanation. Withhold the preferred conclusion where practical, and give the reviewer the evidence. Fresh context can still share model blind spots, so review complements tests and external evidence. The real limit on fan-out is also the capacity to verify. Ten plausible summaries can leave the generalist with more work than it started with. Source artifacts and explicit uncertainty make each finding easier to check and reconcile. As evidence arrives, database and network checks may converge on the same bottleneck. The generalist can combine their findings and cancel redundant branches. Adaptive delegation research proposes this flexibility; its benefit still needs validation on the actual workload. Trace each contract, tool call, artifact, and result under the parent task. Propagate cancellation and release reservations. Preserve partial results for recovery without resetting budgets or treating unfinished output as verified. Tool discovery is not an access grant. Enforce permissions on every call. Exclusive internal data can stay behind a service that returns only authorized results. Subagents must not inherit broader credentials or use retrieved content to change policy.

sections.title: Test whether the boundary adds value
sections.text: Compare the generalist, generalist with delegation, and any existing specialist system. Give them equivalent useful knowledge, state access, tools, and model capabilities. Use held-out tasks within and across domains. At matched budgets, measure quality, latency, total cost, and recovery failures—including discovery, retries, and verification. Then measure what extra spend buys. If specialists win, isolate the cause. Supply the generalist with the same relevant context; then test separate execution and parallelism. If the gap persists, block migration while addressing the measured limitation. The proposed architecture must meet the required quality and latency targets. Re-evaluate after model upgrades. Experiments with long-running agents found that stronger models reduced the need for some scaffolding, while evaluation still helped on harder tasks. Retire orchestration that no longer earns its cost.

sections.title: Use one harness across product surfaces
sections.text: Customer-facing, personal, team, and internal operations agents can share this generalist design. Separate their identities, credentials, memory, and execution environments as required. Multi-tenant and dedicated deployments can reuse the harness while enforcing distinct access boundaries. Keep expertise reusable, ownership coherent, and delegation temporary. Optional delegation contract This illustrative contract describes one dynamic subagent execution. Subagent mechanisms supply the execution primitives; the runtime enforces the policy. Numeric limits are examples to tune through evaluation. # Illustrative policy and request, not a specific SDK schema. runtime_policy: creation: primary_agent_only contract_scope: current_parent_task lifetime: until_completion_timeout_or_parent_termination max_concurrent_subagents: 2 max_total_launches: 4 # Includes retries. max_depth: 1 # Subagents cannot delegate. budget_source: parent_task require_reservation: true permission_ceiling: parent_grants propagate_cancellation: true delegation_request: objective: Check whether the release changed connection pool behavior model_class: strong reasoning_effort: high context: explicit_authorized_evidence tools: [deployments.diff, metrics.query, logs.search] actions: read_only memory: task_artifacts_only limits: timeout_seconds: 120 max_tool_calls: 12 max_output_tokens: 2000 result: [findings, evidence, counterevidence, uncertainty, status] The runtime rejects requests outside policy, accounts for aggregate usage, and records the effective contract. Output limits do not replace a total token or spend budget. Subagent results remain evidence for the primary agent to evaluate. The runtime checks the contract before creating a subagent. This example shows admission, rejection, and completion under the same policy. Admitted Budget exhausted Access denied Parent canceled

sections.title: Admitted
sections.text: The runtime reserves capacity, creates a temporary execution, and returns evidence for the primary agent to verify.

sections.title: Budget exhausted
sections.text: No capacity can be reserved. No subagent is created; the primary agent must continue within the remaining limits.

sections.title: Access denied
sections.text: The requested tool exceeds the parent task’s authority. Delegation cannot expand permissions.

sections.title: Parent canceled
sections.text: The subagent stops, unused capacity is released, and partial results remain marked incomplete.

sections.title: A decision you can make before delegation
sections.text: Task shape First choice Reason to change One evolving diagnosis, shared evidence One generalist and deterministic tools A separable investigation has a precise return contract Independent inspections of disjoint modules Bounded temporary children Integration cost or conflicting assumptions erase the time saved Repeated mechanical transformation Ordinary code Inputs genuinely require judgment A delegation that loses: three children inspect the same flaky integration test with incomplete logs, each proposes a different cause, and the parent repeats all three investigations. Parallel activity increased cost without producing independent evidence. Measure accepted work after integration, not completed child messages. Default to depth one, shared harness behavior, explicit deadlines, and a parent-owned final decision.

title: The Quality Flywheel
description: How failures become experiments, better decisions, and knowledge that survives the next release.
text: The tests pass. A change goes live. Websites stop responding. A quality flywheel begins with the gap between those three sentences. What did the tests miss? Which change would prevent a repeat? How do we know the proposed fix will help somewhere beyond the original failure?

sections.title: Preface
sections.text: Our starting point is Cloudflare's outage on 2 July 2019 . A new security rule consumed so much processing time that websites returned errors. The rule had passed its tests; those tests did not cover the way it could exhaust CPU. The outage and Cloudflare's account are real. Atlas, the on-call AI assistant we use to explore the lessons, is hypothetical. Its examples ask a practical question: how would we teach an assistant to investigate a slow or unavailable website, then verify that it had learned something useful? The chapters follow that question through measurement, investigation, hill climbing, release, and the knowledge left behind. Inside this collection

title: Classifiers When labels become decisions
description: Ten chapters on designing categories, choosing evidence, measuring errors, and deciding when a label deserves to influence what happens next.
text: A classifier turns an untidy situation into a small number of names. That compression makes a support queue sortable, an incident searchable, or an agent's behavior measurable. It also gives downstream systems something they may trust more than they should. Imagine a concert ticket hidden by an email filter. Urgent wording and an unfamiliar sender produced a suspicious label; a downstream policy moved the email out of sight. The machinery worked as designed. The person still missed something important. The challenge is larger than selecting a model. Someone has to decide what suspicious means, which evidence supports it, when the decision must arrive, and how to discover that the classifier is wrong. Those choices determine whether a label becomes useful knowledge or a repeatable mistake.

sections.title: The instrument behind the number
sections.text: These chapters treat a classifier as a measurement instrument embedded in a decision process. A rule, a trained model, a prompt, and an investigating agent can all produce categories. Each needs a defined question, a source of evidence, and a way to test its answer. The collection moves from design to measurement and then to change over time. It connects label definitions with software contracts, ground truth with provenance, confidence with evidence, and dashboards with the history of the instruments that produced them. The examples are illustrative. Their numbers are chosen to make the reasoning inspectable: a detector with 99% accuracy that finds no failures, an unchanged detector whose alerts become less reliable, and a multi-label answer that is partly correct while missing the decisive cause. title: How intelligence finds its way
description: Five essays on the worlds intelligence can read, the questions it asks, the experience it carries, and the actions it can afford to try.
text: An intelligent system still has to find its way through an unfamiliar situation. It needs to encounter useful evidence, recognise which question matters, and decide whether something that worked before belongs here. The environment shapes those possibilities. Names and indexes make some explanations easy to discover. Examples carry assumptions that can outlive their usefulness. Procedures preserve both sound dependencies and old conveniences. The consequences of an action determine whether a mistaken idea can become another attempt. These five essays follow that movement from discovery to action. Each begins with a concrete problem and develops a design choice you can examine in your own systems. The opening chapter includes a worked hierarchy and index examples for progressive disclosure. The chapters can also be read independently. Their shared question is how to give intelligence enough grounding to exercise judgment when the next problem differs from the last.

title: Checkpoint Replay for Long-Horizon Agent Evaluation
description: Evaluate a 24-hour soak at recorded checkpoints. Restore the evidence and agent state available at each moment, then test the decisions.
text: An order-processing service passes its first hour under load. Six hours later, connections are accumulating. At twelve hours, requests begin waiting for the pool. By hour twenty-four, checkout is returning 5XX responses and the storefront is timing out. Now change one instruction in the reviewing agent. Must the entire soak test run for another day to find out whether that helped? Long-horizon evaluation has an environment-time problem. Some failures need a full traffic cycle, repeated batch jobs, or slow resource accumulation to become visible. The model may reason for only minutes while the scenario takes twenty-four hours to unfold. Ten agent variants, each tested three times against a fresh 24-hour run, require 720 scenario-hours. Parallel runs reduce elapsed time, but each still needs its soak period and infrastructure.

sections.title: Record the progression, restore the checkpoint
sections.text: In my work on agent evaluation, we built replay infrastructure to revisit recorded scenarios. A 24-hour soak is a useful extension of that design: capture the evolving evidence once, then evaluate agents at selected checkpoints. At T+6h, reconstruct the workspace as it was available then. Expose the corresponding telemetry, logs, topology, deployment state, and time. Restore the appropriate agent history and scratch state. Let the agent investigate using its usual interfaces, backed by the recording. The harness then prepares T+12h. We are taking the agent to a particular point in the scenario. We are not asking a live database, queue, or connection pool to run twelve hours of behavior in a few seconds. Model inference and tool execution still take real time. The recording preserves the progression. Replay removes the need to reproduce the waiting period for every comparison. Other tasks have the same shape. A document-processing agent may wait overnight for a batch to finish. A research agent may revisit a claim when a new source arrives the next day. In each case, the evaluation must restore the information available at the decision point.

sections.title: A checkpoint includes what the agent could know
sections.text: Metrics alone are insufficient. A checkpoint needs the environment view, the agent’s relevant state, and the tool contracts used to read them. AgentRewind explores aligned checkpoints of agent context and controlled environment state for recovery. Evaluation has a related requirement, with an extra constraint: later knowledge must stay out of an earlier trial. For example, an error occurred at 11:58 but its log arrived at 12:04. An agent at noon could not have read it. Faithful replay checks both event time and availability time. Future samples, later topology changes, postmortems, and outcome labels must also remain inaccessible. The same cutoff must govern files, query results, service APIs, and the agent’s view of “now.” CLI shims or HTTP proxies can route tool requests to replay services; network isolation prevents an unanswered request from silently reaching live infrastructure. Missing evidence must appear as a coverage gap. Consider this illustrative connection leak. An hourly reconciliation job leaves connections checked out in the new checkout revision. Database execution stays fast; obtaining a connection gradually becomes the bottleneck. 24-hour soak / checkpoint inspection

sections.title: Separate a checkpoint probe from a trajectory test
sections.text: A checkpoint probe gives every candidate the same fixed history and world state at T+12h. It asks which agent makes the better decision from that starting point. A trajectory replay starts earlier and lets each candidate carry its own reports, memory, and scratch files through successive checkpoints. It tests whether the agent remembers a concern, seeks discriminating evidence, and changes its assessment. Do not splice one candidate’s earlier conclusions into another’s trajectory. Repeated trials still matter: reproducible inputs do not make model outputs deterministic. Anthropic’s evaluation guidance emphasizes multiple trials, isolated environments, and the distinction between an agent’s transcript and the outcome it actually achieved. Use healthy recordings too; recommending intervention in every healthy run should not score well.

sections.title: Know where the recording ends
sections.text: Captured raw events support more queries than a transcript of fixed API responses. Even then, unrecorded evidence remains unavailable. Keep replay recommendations isolated from production actions. If a candidate recommends stopping the reconciliation job at hour twelve, a recording with that job still running cannot prove what happens after the intervention. Evaluating intervention effects requires a suitable simulator or controlled live experiment. Scheduled checkpoints also bound what you can say about detection time. The point is to make a slow scenario reusable while preserving the information available at each decision. We can then improve the investigation without waiting another day for the same failure to develop. Local context for autonomous agents describes the data layer that makes these reconstructed workspaces practical.

sections.title: Test the boundary with a late record
sections.text: In the engineering workbench , checkpoint filters on both event_time and available_at . A record about 09:00 that arrives at 11:00 must remain invisible to a 10:00 decision. The test suite also checks timezone requirements and equality at the cutoff. bundle/ manifest.json # scenario, checkpoint, source versions, hashes evidence.jsonl # event_time and available_at on every record state.json # candidate-owned progress and prior actions expected.json # evaluator-only assertions, never agent input Keep expected judgments outside the agent’s accessible directory. Save the candidate’s own trajectory between checkpoints; do not splice in a baseline’s private reasoning. If the candidate changes an external action, a fixed recorded future is no longer evidence of what would happen. Use a simulator or a new controlled run for that causal question.

title: Local Context for Autonomous Agents
description: Put telemetry, logs, and topology beside the agent. Use PromQL and files to keep retrieval reliable and model context focused.
text: Checkout latency is rising. An agent needs to compare revisions, inspect connection errors, and trace the downstream dependency. Before it can investigate, it has to navigate several observability tools, their schemas, and their failure modes. We can design that environment differently: make the relevant data locally available, behind a small, stable interface. Telemetry through PromQL. Logs through files. Topology through a versioned snapshot. Let ordinary code prepare the evidence, so the agent can spend its turns interpreting it.

sections.title: Available to the agent does not mean inside the prompt
sections.text: A workspace can hold millions of log lines while the model reads twenty. The distinction is between execution context —data the agent can access—and model context —tokens it must process to decide what to do next. Loading every tool definition and every intermediate result into model context blurs that distinction. In one published configuration, Anthropic counted roughly 55,000 tokens across 58 tools from five MCP servers , before the conversation began. Similar tools also increase the opportunities to choose the wrong interface or supply the wrong arguments. MCP remains useful for connecting systems. The avoidable cost comes from eagerly presenting the whole integration surface to the model. Tool discovery and programmatic execution already offer ways to reduce it: Anthropic’s code-execution approach loads definitions as needed and processes intermediate data outside the prompt. Cloudflare’s Code Mode likewise lets an agent compose MCP operations through code. Local context takes a complementary step: materialize the working data near the agent, so successive questions can reuse it without successive provider calls.

sections.title: Collect once, investigate repeatedly
sections.text: In my work on agent infrastructure, this led to an embedded time-series store. The broader architecture is a local context layer; the database is one part of it. A deterministic collector loads the relevant services and recent time window. Provider adapters own authentication, pagination, retries, and normalization. They preserve metric types, units, and labels. Logs can be partitioned into newline-delimited JSON files; topology and deployment configuration can be captured as versioned JSON. “Deterministic” describes the collection procedure: explicit resources, time ranges, and transformations. Live data can still change. Reproducing a query requires a captured dataset and fixed evaluation semantics. The same pattern applies beyond observability: a research agent can query a local paper index and read PDFs; a coding agent can search a checked-out repository and inspect test artifacts. The collector changes; the separation between accessible data and selected model context stays useful. The agent gets a manifest of coverage and freshness, a catalog of available metrics, and a compact access interface. Our telemetry design uses temporary local chunks, memory mapping, and an embedded PromQL engine. Complete chunks are published atomically for readers; there is no separate database daemon to operate per session. The useful contract is small enough to understand at a glance: A local context interface Evidence Local representation How the agent reads it Telemetry Indexed time series PromQL selectors, rates, and aggregates Logs NDJSON files by service and time rg / jq, with bounded excerpts Topology & config Versioned JSON snapshots Read files and follow dependency edges Coverage Manifest and metric catalog Check time windows, labels, freshness, and gaps Investigation trace

sections.title: From a 5XX spike to a shared dependency
sections.text: An illustrative workspace with a fifteen-minute window. Query results and observations are examples, not production measurements. 01 Query telemetry 02 Read local logs 03 Trace topology Query telemetry New revision 8 errors/s Control revision 0.1 errors/s

sections.title: Locate the failing revision
sections.text: What happens A local PromQL query shows that checkout 5XX responses concentrate in the new revision. Its request rate is comparable to the control. What it means The deployment is a lead. The error rate alone does not identify the failing dependency. What the system does Return a small aggregate, then inspect matching logs in the same window. Inspect the example record { "snapshot": "checkout-window-07", "evaluation_time": "10:15 UTC", "query": "sum by (revision) (rate(http_requests_total{service=\"checkout\",status=~\"5..\"}[5m]))", "result_unit": "errors/second", "result_rows": 2, "additional_provider_calls": 0 } Read local logs Repeated error pool_timeout Affected dependency orders-db

sections.title: Follow the pool timeouts
sections.text: What happens The mounted log file contains connection-pool timeouts for orders-db. The agent reads a bounded excerpt and keeps the path for follow-up queries. What it means The bottleneck may be connection acquisition inside checkout. A database-related error does not by itself establish a database outage. What the system does Search the existing file, then compare pool occupancy with database health. Inspect the example record { "file": "/context/logs/checkout/10-00.ndjson", "command": "rg -n -m 20 'pool_timeout' /context/logs/checkout/10-00.ndjson", "output_byte_limit": 8192, "additional_provider_calls": 0 } Trace topology Database query latency Stable Checkout pool At capacity

sections.title: Separate the cause from its upstream impact
sections.text: What happens The topology snapshot connects storefront to checkout and checkout to orders-db. Database query latency stays flat, while the new checkout revision exhausts its pool. Storefront sees the resulting timeouts. What it means Connection handling in checkout is a stronger hypothesis than a slow database. Upstream errors are part of the impact, not independent proof of another failure. What the system does Record the evidence and request a historical baseline only if the local manifest says it is missing. Inspect the example record { "topology": "/context/topology/services.v42.json", "query": "max by (revision) (db_pool_in_use{service=\"checkout\"})", "missing_baseline": "targeted fetch through collector", "retrieval_failure": "explicit coverage gap", "additional_provider_calls_for_loaded_data": 0 } 1 of 3 Previous Next

sections.title: Remove remote failure modes from the inner loop
sections.text: Once a window is loaded, querying it cannot fail because a provider token expired, a remote API was rate-limited, or pagination broke halfway through that query. Those concerns belong to ingestion and refresh, where ordinary code can handle them consistently. This removes avoidable tool-call failures from repeated analysis. It does not make every query correct: an agent can still select the wrong metric, misread a counter, or overlook missing coverage. A smaller interface should expose those errors clearly. The Prometheus query model provides useful semantics for time selection and evaluation; a local implementation must document the subset it supports. Keep the working set bounded. Prefetch likely evidence, hydrate missing ranges deliberately, and give queries output and resource limits. A manifest should say what is absent or stale. Read-only source data and separate scratch space keep exploration from altering the evidence.

sections.title: Measure the whole investigation
sections.text: Compare tool-definition tokens, result tokens, failed remote calls, time to first useful evidence, and task success. Include initial hydration and refresh costs. A faster local query is valuable only if the complete investigation improves. The architectural payoff is a clean separation: collectors handle data movement, local interfaces handle selection, and the model handles interpretation. Rich context can remain within reach without occupying the entire conversation. The same arrangement supports checkpoint replay for long-horizon evaluation : give the agent a workspace reconstructed for a particular moment, then observe what it decides.

sections.title: Freeze a small local evidence package
sections.text: A minimal package needs four files: manifest.json , logs.ndjson , metrics.csv , and topology.json . The manifest names source queries, collection time, covered interval, scope, truncation, and file hashes. Keep event time separate from availability time so later ingestion cannot silently alter an earlier checkpoint. manifest: { snapshot_id, collected_at, interval, scopes, missing_scopes, files: [{path, sha256, rows}] } query receipt: { snapshot_id, expression, supported_semantics, rows, complete } Specify which PromQL operators, staleness rules, and counter-reset behavior the local evaluator supports. Reject unsupported expressions instead of approximating them silently. Compare local results with source queries on a small known interval. Measure collection, indexing, query execution, and model consumption together; reducing one prompt does not establish a lower total investigation cost.

title: Trustworthy Autonomy
description: Nine principles for systems that deserve the authority we give them. A field guide to evidence, boundaries, and learning from consequences.
text: Trustworthy autonomy is the discipline of building systems whose freedom to act is supported by evidence, explicit authority, and accountability for what follows. An agent may diagnose an outage correctly and still act beyond its permission. It may quote an accurate metric from the wrong hour. It may remember a “successful” parser whose output later failed reconciliation. These are different failures. Asking the agent to be careful leaves too much unspecified.

sections.title: What makes authority deserved?
sections.text: Trust begins with reasons: what the system knows, how it knows it, and where its understanding ends. It also requires boundaries: who may decide, who may change state, and what happens when those conditions stop holding. The philosophy becomes practical when each promise has a mechanism. A claim carries its evidence. A state update checks its owner and version. An action passes through a permission boundary. A verdict eventually meets an independent outcome. This collection develops that architecture through nine principles. Each chapter starts with a concrete situation and follows the principle into a working example. Inside this collection

sections.title: Verdicts require Epistemics
sections.text: Every conclusion carries its justification, uncertainty, alternatives, and conditions for reassessment. 5 min read ↗ 02

sections.title: Evidence requires Provenance
sections.text: Every material claim keeps a trail back to its source, transformations, and limitations. 4 min read ↗ 03

sections.title: State requires Ownership
sections.text: Every persistent fact has an authoritative owner, a version, and rules for how it can change. 4 min read ↗ 04

sections.title: Autonomy requires a Dial
sections.text: Authority is explicit, specific to each action, proportionate to risk, and revocable. 4 min read ↗ 05

sections.title: Inputs require a Trust Boundary
sections.text: Evidence remains data. Permissions and policy arrive through separate, authenticated control paths. 4 min read ↗ 06

sections.title: Knowledge requires a Clock
sections.text: Every decision-relevant fact records when it was true, when it was learned, and when it must be reconsidered. 4 min read ↗ 07

sections.title: Delegation requires Ceilings
sections.text: Delegated authority narrows, and shared limits bound the cost and impact of the entire agent tree. 4 min read ↗ 08

sections.title: Failure requires a Ladder
sections.text: Partial failures lead to explicit degraded modes that preserve essential safety and expose missing evidence. 4 min read ↗ 09

sections.title: Learning requires Outcomes
