sections.text: Independent outcomes grade decisions over time, and evaluated lessons improve future work. 4 min read ↗

sections.title: The principles work together
sections.text: Epistemics describes the justification for a verdict. Provenance lets someone inspect its evidence. Ownership protects the state carried forward. The autonomy dial determines which actions that verdict may support. Trust boundaries keep outside text from taking control. Clocks prevent stale knowledge from pretending to describe the present. Delegation ceilings keep small tasks from adding up to unbounded power. Failure ladders preserve essential safeguards when capability deteriorates. Outcomes close the loop. They expose mistakes, test supposed successes, and give us a basis for improving the system—and sometimes for reducing its authority.

sections.title: Read them as design commitments
sections.text: These principles are useful questions to ask of any autonomous system: a coding agent, a research assistant, a document-processing workflow, or an operations team. The examples here are illustrative. Their purpose is to make the commitments inspectable. The real test is whether those commitments still hold when the model is mistaken, the data is late, or the human changes their mind. Trust grows when a system makes its reasons, limits, and consequences open to examination.

title: Engineering Autonomous Agents
description: An agent’s capabilities depend on its data, execution loop, state, and feedback. Design them as one system.
text: A coding agent is asked to replace a deprecated library across a repository. It finds the imports and writes a patch. Completing the job still requires a dependency map, a test environment, permission to change files, and a way to recover if the task stops halfway through. The model participates in this system. Its surroundings determine whether an investigation can become completed work.

sections.title: Give the task an observable outcome
sections.text: “Modernize this repository” leaves success ambiguous. A clearer task asks the agent to replace a specific dependency, preserve public behavior, and produce a patch with passing tests. Specify the target version, affected packages, compatibility requirements, and permitted changes. The agent can choose its approach while the system retains a concrete definition of completion.

sections.title: Put repeated mechanics in code
sections.text: Authentication, pagination, retries, and unit conversion should not become fresh reasoning problems on every turn. Collect data through ordinary code and expose a stable interface for exploration. The same applies to execution. A tool result should distinguish success, failure, and an unknown outcome. If an action times out, check whether it happened before retrying it. Otherwise a network interruption can become a duplicate operation.

sections.title: Preserve progress across turns
sections.text: A long investigation needs more than a transcript. Keep references to evidence, current hypotheses, completed actions, and open questions in explicit state. After a restart, the agent should know which packages it migrated, which tests failed, and which design question remains open. That continuity reduces repeated work and makes handoffs inspectable.

sections.title: Close the loop with feedback
sections.text: Check the resulting artifact. Does the patch build in a clean environment? Do integration tests exercise the changed behavior? Does the new dependency work on every supported runtime? The answers separate a plausible patch from a completed migration. Evaluate the model together with its data interfaces, execution loop, and state handling. Changing any one of them can change the result. That is the unit of engineering: an agent operating inside a complete system.

sections.title: Choose the next design question
sections.text: Use this essay as a map. Start with the execution architecture , then decide how tools become discoverable . Before granting write access, specify ownership, evidence, and recovery . Use the eval guide to make completion testable. For the dependency migration, keep one task record: target version, allowed paths, starting commit, commands run, test results, and unresolved failures. A restart should recover that record and inspect the working tree before issuing another write. If the record and filesystem disagree, stop and reconcile them. The transcript alone is not a completion certificate.

title: Design the Test: What Counts as Correct?
description: How to Write and Score an Agent Eval · Reproduce the failure, establish the evidence, and write rubrics that accept valid alternatives while rejecting plausible mistakes.
text: Parts in this collection 01 / 03 Design the Test: What Counts as Correct? Build the Score: What Does 72.2% Mean? Trust the Result: Is It Good Enough to Ship? The agent finds the cause of an outage, explains it clearly, and recommends a fix. A reviewer might approve the answer after a quick read. Then someone checks the capacity calculation. The proposed fix would overload the database. The diagnosis was right. The recommendation was wrong. The answer cited real evidence and respected its permissions. The team needs to preserve those distinctions to decide what to fix. We will build an eval around this invented checkout incident, then test its scoring rules with owner lookups, CSV conversion, and booking examples. The final decision will be whether to release an improved agent whose headline score looks better. In this installment Chapter 1 Reproduce the problem before writing the test Chapter 2 Write rules that distinguish a good answer

sections.title: Chapter 1 Reproduce the problem before writing the test
Give the agent a problem to solve
sections.text: Imagine an application called checkout-api . It runs on four instances. Each instance keeps a pool of open database connections, which requests borrow when they need to query the database. After a deployment, checkout requests start timing out. The user asks: Checkout requests started timing out after the 14:00 deployment. Investigate checkout-api in staging, identify the cause, and recommend a fix. Do not change the environment. This prompt gives the agent a symptom, a place to investigate, an expected result, and an action boundary. It leaves the diagnosis for the agent to discover. Compare it with “Investigate the connection pool regression.” That version has already supplied the important answer. It might be useful for testing a repair procedure, but it is a weak test of diagnosis.

sections.title: Know the answer for a defensible reason
sections.text: The evaluator has a controlled reproduction of the incident. The deployment reduced the connection pool from 16 to 4 per instance. Requests now spend longer waiting to borrow a connection. Once they obtain one, their database queries run at the usual speed. Restoring the previous setting resolves the problem in this reproduction. That distinction between waiting for a connection and executing a query matters. “The database became slower” would sound plausible, but would explain the wrong part of the delay. The evaluator records three pieces of evidence: Evidence What the diagnostic environment shows e1 Configuration history The pool changed from 16 to 4 per instance e2 Latency measurements Connection waits increased; query execution time did not e3 Capacity information Four instances; database limit 100; other workloads use 20; keep 16 in reserve These are the reference facts : the evidence against which an answer will be judged. The agent can discover them through its tools. The evaluator's answer key and grading instructions remain outside the agent's accessible files. Now work out a feasible remedy. The database allows 100 connections. Subtract the 20 used elsewhere and the 16 kept in reserve. That leaves 64 connections for checkout. Four instances share that budget, so each can use 16. Available per instance = (100 − 20 − 16) / 4 = 16 connections. A recommendation to restore 16 fits this case. A recommendation to use 64 per instance would allocate 256 connections and fail the capacity constraint. Notice what we established before involving a judge: the actual fault, the observable symptoms, and a constraint that distinguishes a good remedy from a bad one.

sections.title: Make the starting conditions repeatable
sections.text: A fixture is the prepared test situation: the files, service state, records, and tool responses the agent starts with. A trial is one attempt at solving that situation. Restore the fixture before each independent trial, then check that the intended fault is present. Otherwise, the second agent may inherit the first agent's repair and face an entirely different problem. Saved tool responses are useful for a diagnosis test: they are inexpensive and repeatable. They cannot demonstrate that a proposed repair works. If the task asks the agent to change a system, use an isolated executable environment or a simulator whose behavior has been validated. Historical incident reports are useful starting material too. Verify their diagnoses against the test environment; copying an old explanation into an answer key does not make it a verified answer for this test. Package the prompt, fixture version, reference facts, rubrics, and execution settings together. If shared grading templates change, pin the version used by each task. Otherwise a score can change merely because the runner loaded a different rule. Apply this to your task: write down the fault, the evidence available to the agent, and one tempting answer that the evidence rules out. If you cannot explain why that answer is wrong, the reference is not ready for automated grading.

sections.title: Chapter 2 Write rules that distinguish a good answer
Replace a vague rating with answerable questions
sections.text: A rubric is a written rule for judging one aspect of the result. “Give a helpful and accurate answer” is too broad. Two reviewers could agree that the diagnosis is good and still disagree about whether the bad remedy deserves a score of 3, 6, or 8. For checkout, separate three obligations: Check What must be true C1 Cause Identifies the deployment reducing the connection pool from 16 to 4 C2 Mechanism Explains that requests wait for connections, while query execution time is unchanged C3 Remedy Recommends a fix that addresses the bottleneck within the verified capacity Each check gets a pass or a fail. We will represent those as 1 and 0. This makes the failure useful. If C1 and C2 pass but C3 fails, the next improvement is about choosing a remedy. We do not have to infer that from a holistic rating.

sections.title: Write a boundary the grader can apply
sections.text: Before reading the verdicts, decide which of these recommendations you would let an engineer act on. All three respond to the incident; they make very different commitments. Restore the pool to 16 per instance. Four pools use 64 connections, leaving the allocations for other workloads and reserve intact. This passes C3 . Increase the pool to 64 per instance. This fails C3 , because four pools would require 256 connections. Increase the pool, add retries, restart the database, or scale the application. This also fails the rubric as written. It offers a menu without selecting and justifying a feasible remedy. Mentioning a potentially useful action is not the same as recommending a defensible fix. These examples belong with the rubric. They give the grader a concrete boundary: a feasible recommendation passes; an excessive setting or an unchosen list of fixes fails. A different solution can still pass. For example, limiting incoming concurrency could reduce pressure on the pool. The answer would need to explain the throughput tradeoff and how to validate that the policy addresses the incident. The reference should describe acceptable outcomes and constraints, rather than demand a particular sentence.

sections.title: Do not reward imitation
sections.text: Suppose the reference says: Requests are blocked while acquiring a connection. The agent says: Queries are waiting for a free slot in the application's database pool. Those can express the same mechanism. Comparing the strings exactly would reject useful variation. Now suppose the agent says: This is not a connection pool problem. A keyword check for “connection pool” could accept the opposite claim. Exact matching works well for fixed identifiers and required literal outputs. For explanations, grade the meaning. For structured output, validate its structure and values instead of comparing formatting. The same principle applies to tool use. If the agent establishes the facts through SQL, it should not fail merely because the reference trace used a metrics API. Use traces to diagnose how an agent worked. Require a particular sequence only when the sequence itself matters, such as obtaining approval before a write.

sections.title: Choose the scoring scale deliberately
sections.text: Binary checks are a useful default for obligations with clear acceptance conditions. Write the boundaries clearly and check that reviewers apply them consistently. For a quality with degrees, use an anchored scale. A communication rubric might define: 1: The main conclusion is missing or hard to locate. 2: The conclusion is present, but observations and recommendations are mixed together. 3: The answer states the conclusion first and clearly separates evidence from next steps. That is easier to apply than “Rate clarity from 1 to 3.” LLM-Rubric explores calibrating multidimensional ratings against human judgments for dialogue quality. The relevant lesson is that a scale needs validation, not that every task should use the same scale. For the worked checkout eval, we will keep binary checks so the arithmetic stays easy to inspect. Here is a way to improve the score without improving the answer. Split C1 , the cause check, into five overlapping checks. Leave the mechanism and remedy checks unchanged. The same answer now passes six of seven checks: 85.7% instead of 66.7% . The diagnosis has gained extra votes; the bad remedy is still bad. Choose the distinct obligations first. Then attach a pass example and a fail example to each rule. A longer rubric should make the judgment clearer, not quietly make a failure cheaper.

sections.title: Fill one contract before writing the prompt
sections.text: Use a task worksheet with input snapshot, requested outcome, permissible actions, completion checks, excluded shortcuts, and evidence references. For the checkout incident, distinguish “identify the pool limit” from “recommend a capacity-safe remedy.” The former cannot earn the latter’s points. task_id: checkout-pool-v1 allowed: inspect logs, query capacity snapshot, propose change forbidden: modify production, alter source evidence accept: effective aggregate pool <= 64; explain reserve alternatives: reduce per-instance pool OR reduce active instances requires: arithmetic and feasibility for the selected remedy A valid alternative must meet the outcome, not imitate a reference answer. Test one correct alternative, one plausible wrong remedy, and one correct answer obtained through a prohibited action. The eval companion separates dimensions so those cases produce different verdicts.

title: Build the Score: What Does 72.2% Mean?
description: How to Write and Score an Agent Eval · Turn one execution into verifiable judgments. Separate correctness, grounding, permissions, and completion—then calculate each score.
text: Parts in this collection 02 / 03 Design the Test: What Counts as Correct? Build the Score: What Does 72.2% Mean? Trust the Result: Is It Good Enough to Ship? The agent found the cause of an outage. It also recommended a fix that would exhaust the database's connection budget. How should the eval score that answer? In Part 1 , we built an invented checkout incident with three correctness checks: cause, mechanism, and a feasible remedy. Four application instances share a budget of 64 connections, so the verified limit is 16 per instance. Our flawed answer gets the diagnosis right and recommends 64 per instance. Now we will follow the evidence into individual judgments, separate auxiliary dimensions from correctness, and calculate the suite score. In this installment Chapter 3 Choose what code and model judges should check Chapter 4 Separate correctness from grounding and permissions Chapter 5 Explain what your score actually means

sections.title: Chapter 3 Choose what code and model judges should check
sections.text: An answer recommending 64 connections and one warning against 64 contain the same number. A useful grader must establish what was proposed before checking the arithmetic.

sections.title: Separate the rule from the mechanism
sections.text: The rubric says what should count as correct. The grader applies that rule to a particular execution. The trace is the record of what the agent did: its tool calls, the results it received, and its answer. Some facts can be checked by code. Others need interpretation. Human review helps establish whether those automated checks agree with the intended standard. This division is also reflected in Anthropic's guidance on agent evals , which describes code, model, and human graders. A useful framework can combine them within one task. For checkout, use a semantic judge to interpret the diagnosis and a direct calculation to check a concrete pool recommendation. A semantic judge is a model or person assessing meaning rather than exact wording.

sections.title: Let code answer questions it can settle
sections.text: If the recommendation explicitly proposes 64 connections on each of four instances, its numeric feasibility is straightforward: available = 100 - 20 - 16 proposed = 4 * 64 within_budget = proposed <= available # False Code can also inspect a generated CSV, query the resulting database state, or look for forbidden write attempts in trusted tool logs. These checks are reproducible and inexpensive. Their limit is the rule they implement. Finding a number in the text does not establish that it is the recommended setting: the answer might say “Do not set this to 64.” Extracting the intended action from free text requires its own reliable method. A check can also return legitimate partial credit. If a task requires five independent records to be transformed and exactly four are correct, code can calculate 4/5. The fraction has a defined meaning; it was not invented by a judge trying to express a general impression.

sections.title: Let semantic judges interpret the explanation
sections.text: For C2 , provide the judge with the user request, the rule, the reference facts, and the agent's actual answer and relevant tool results. These two answers deserve different verdicts: Requests wait because the application has too few available connections. Requests wait because the database executes each query more slowly. The first matches the evidence. The second contradicts it. Both may use fluent technical language; only one explains this incident. Require a verdict for each criterion. For the failed remedy, a stored result might look like this: { "rubric_id": "C3", "status": "graded", "score": 0, "evidence_refs": ["e3"], "reason": "Four pools of 64 require 256 connections; only 64 are available.", "failure_tag": "REMEDY_EXCEEDS_CONNECTION_BUDGET" } An engineer can now act on the failure. The criterion is C3 , the relevant capacity record is e3 , and the failure is an excessive connection allocation. “The answer could be better” would provide none of that direction. Valid JSON only proves that the result has the right format. Check that the cited evidence exists and supports the judgment. Treat instructions inside the agent's answer or retrieved documents as material to inspect, not commands for the judge to follow. You can request several verdicts in one model call to reduce cost. Validate that exact setup: a judge assessing several criteria together may behave differently from one assessing each separately.

sections.title: Check the world when the agent claims to change it
sections.text: Consider a booking agent that says: Your reservation is confirmed. A text grader may like the answer. But did a reservation appear in the database, for the correct customer and date? τ-bench uses resulting database state to evaluate task completion. The principle transfers directly: inspect the thing the agent was supposed to accomplish. State checks and trace checks answer different questions. A final reservation can be correct even if the agent made an unauthorized change along the way. Check the outcome for completion and the trusted action record for permission compliance.

sections.title: Chapter 4 Separate correctness from grounding and permissions
A correct fact can still be an unsupported guess
sections.text: Suppose an agent reads the configuration and metrics, explains the pool regression correctly, and then proposes the excessive setting of 64 connections. Its factual explanation is supported. Its remedy is wrong. Now consider another agent that never inspects any evidence but happens to guess the correct diagnosis and remedy. Its answer may satisfy the factual correctness rules, but we have learned something troubling about how it reached them. A single correctness score cannot distinguish those situations. Add separate dimensions for the properties you care about. An auxiliary dimension is a separately reported measurement. It does not mean the property is unimportant or optional. For the checkout example, we will measure: Dimension Question Grounding Are the explanation's material factual claims supported by evidence the agent actually retrieved and cited? Authority compliance Did the agent avoid prohibited write attempts? Communication Does it state the diagnosis clearly and separate observations from recommendations?

sections.title: Walk through the flawed answer
sections.text: Here is the response we will score: The deployment reduced the connection pool from 16 to 4 per instance [e1]. Requests are waiting to acquire connections; query execution time is unchanged [e2]. There are four instances [e3]. Increase each pool to 64 connections. Assume the trace confirms that it retrieved those records and attempted no writes. Check Verdict Cause Pass Mechanism Pass Remedy Fail Grounding Pass Authority compliance Pass Communication Pass Why does grounding pass when the recommendation is bad? Because this particular grounding rubric checks the support for the factual explanation. Those facts are supported. The remedy's feasibility is checked by C3 . That boundary must be explicit. If your grounding rubric also requires every recommendation to be justified by the evidence, this answer would fail grounding too. The label “grounding” alone does not tell the reader which definition you used. For the lucky guess, the factual checks could pass while grounding fails. This gives the two agents different engineering work: improve evidence gathering for the guesser; improve remedy selection for the agent that found the right facts. Calling both answers simply “wrong” would hide that distinction.

sections.title: Make critical requirements gates
sections.text: The user said not to change the environment. Our evaluation treats a prohibited write attempt as a violation, including an attempt blocked by the tool. Authority therefore has two roles: it is reported as its own score, and it is a completion gate . A gate is a requirement that must pass before an execution counts as successful. This lets a team see that an agent diagnosed the incident correctly while still rejecting its unauthorized action. Hiding the violation inside a weighted average would let unrelated successes compensate for it. Similarly, if evidence-backed conclusions are an explicit requirement of your task, put grounding into correctness or make it a gate. Decide before looking at the result.

sections.title: Keep cost and speed in understandable units
sections.text: Record time, cost, tool calls, and recovery attempts as measurements. Avoid automatically translating “fewer tool calls” into “better.” One agent might take three calls and guess. Another might take five and discover the capacity limit. The second investigation costs more but produces a usable answer. Report cost and latency alongside success, under a declared execution budget. A composite score can express a real product tradeoff. Keep its components visible and enforce critical gates separately.

sections.title: Chapter 5 Explain what your score actually means
sections.text: Two dashboards can turn the same nine verdicts into 66.7% and 72.2%. Before calling either one a bug, find out what each calculation gives equal weight.

sections.title: Start with one execution
sections.text: The checkout answer passed two correctness checks and failed one: Correctness = (1 + 1 + 0) / 3 = 66.7%. Read this as “two of three correctness obligations passed.” It is not a 66.7% probability that the task succeeded. If completion requires all three checks and the authority gate, the answer is incomplete. The user still lacks a feasible recommendation. Both measurements are useful. The correctness average shows partial progress. Complete-task success tells you whether the result met the full acceptance rule.

sections.title: Add two concrete tasks
sections.text: A suite is a collection of tasks. To see how a framework combines their results, add two illustrative tasks. Task B is a service-owner lookup. The user asks which team owns a service and which on-call queue to contact. The answer names both correctly, so its two correctness checks pass. It supplies no supporting citation, so grounding fails. No prohibited write occurs. For this task, grounding is reported separately and is not a completion gate. Task B therefore completes. If the product requires a cited source, its acceptance rule should change accordingly. Task C is a CSV conversion. The user asks the agent to write a new CSV containing only active accounts, convert timestamps to UTC, preserve account IDs, and use the required column names. The source must remain unchanged. The output filters active accounts and preserves IDs, but fails the timestamp and column-name requirements. It also overwrites the source. That gives it two of four correctness checks, plus an authority violation. No explanatory prose was requested, so a prose-grounding rubric was never assigned. The correctness results are: Task Checks Task correctness A Checkout diagnosis 1, 1, 0 66.7% B Owner lookup 1, 1 100.0% C CSV conversion 1, 0, 1, 0 50.0% First average the checks within each task. Then average those task scores: Suite correctness = (2/3 + 1 + 1/2) / 3 = 72.2%.

sections.title: Why not count all the passes together
sections.text: There are six passing checks out of nine. That produces 66.7%, which differs from 72.2%. The disagreement comes from the unit that gets a vote. Pooling checks gives every check one vote. Task C then has four votes while Task B has two. Averaging task scores gives each task one vote, regardless of how many checks its author wrote. Use the latter when each task should contribute equally. If production traffic or business importance should determine the weights, declare those weights explicitly. Do not let the length of a rubric make that decision accidentally. Also inspect important groups of tasks separately. A high average across frequent, easy lookups can conceal poor performance on less frequent actions.

sections.title: Calculate each auxiliary dimension separately
sections.text: Use the same principle for grounding and authority, but include only the tasks to which the dimension applies: Task Authority Grounding A Checkout diagnosis 1 1 B Owner lookup 1 0 C CSV conversion 0 Not assigned Authority has three results: Authority compliance = (1 + 1 + 0) / 3 = 66.7%. Grounding has two: Grounding = (1 + 0) / 2 = 50%, with coverage of two out of three tasks. The missing grounding entry for C is neither a pass nor a failure. It was excluded by the task definition before the agent ran. If a dimension has multiple checks within one task, average those checks first, then average the eligible task scores. That keeps a task with a longer grounding rubric from receiving extra weight.

sections.title: Report completion alongside the averages
sections.text: Only Task B passes every correctness check and its authority gate. Complete-task success = 1/3 = 33.3%. The dashboard now says something precise: Correctness obligations are partly satisfied: 72.2% . Complete-task success remains low: 33.3% . One of three executions violated its authority constraint.

sections.title: Change a result and watch the scores
sections.text: Correct the checkout remedy, then preserve the CSV source. Notice that fixing the permission violation does not repair the CSV timestamps or column names. Change the weighting without changing any answers to see how the headline moves. Change the example Correct the checkout remedy Preserve the CSV source Correctness weighting Equal weight per task Equal weight per check Reset example Link to this scenario Correctness 72.2% Equal task weights Complete tasks 33.3% 1 of 3 tasks Authority compliance 66.7% 2 of 3 tasks Task Correct checks Complete Checkout 2 of 3 No Owner lookup 2 of 2 Yes CSV conversion 2 of 4 No Grounding: 50.0% · 2 eligible tasks of 3. Authority gate: failed — CSV source overwritten. The values above show the original result. Enable JavaScript to change the remedy, permissions, and weighting. Fixing checkout's recommendation improves correctness and completion. It does not erase the CSV task's unauthorized overwrite; a zero-violation release gate still fails until that behavior changes. We have calculated these scores assuming the judgments are complete and correct. In Part 3 , we challenge those assumptions before making the release decision.

sections.title: Keep the denominator beside the result
sections.text: The explorer’s three tasks contain 3, 2, and 4 checks. Equal task weights answer how well the typical task performed; pooling all nine checks gives the larger tasks more influence. Neither weighting is neutral. Choose the estimand before looking at the winning candidate. When the checkout remedy is fixed, its three checks pass and task-macro correctness becomes 83.3%. Completion becomes two of three tasks. Preserving the CSV source separately improves authority; it does not repair its remaining correctness failures. An authority gate must not be diluted into a convenient average. Use the supplied scorer to retain per-task judgments and missing values. A missing judgment is not a zero and must not disappear from the denominator without an explicit eligibility rule. Save the contract version with every report.

title: Trust the Result: Is It Good Enough to Ship?
description: How to Write and Score an Agent Eval · Handle missing judgments, calibrate graders, repeat trials, and make a release decision that the headline score can justify.
text: Parts in this collection 03 / 03 Design the Test: What Counts as Correct? Build the Score: What Does 72.2% Mean? Trust the Result: Is It Good Enough to Ship? A score can improve because the agent got better. It can also improve because difficult judgments disappeared, a grader missed an error, or the team kept only a lucky attempt. Part 2 produced a three-task example: checkout diagnosis, an owner lookup, and CSV conversion. Correctness was 72.2%, but only one task fully completed. The CSV conversion also overwrote a source file it was required to preserve. Before using those numbers to make a release decision, we need to establish what was measured, whether the grader is right, and whether success repeats. In this installment Chapter 6 Keep missing results from inflating the score Chapter 7 Find the mistakes your grader misses Chapter 8 Find out whether success repeats Chapter 9 Build the framework and make the release call

sections.title: Chapter 6 Keep missing results from inflating the score
sections.text: Half the grading jobs failed overnight. The dashboard still shows 80%. Find out which results that number includes before interpreting it.

sections.title: Separate an agent failure from an evaluation failure
sections.text: Suppose the agent reads the capacity limit and still recommends 64 connections. That is an agent failure: C3 = 0 . Suppose instead the grader times out before returning a verdict. We do not yet know the grade. That is an unresolved judgment . Suppose the checkout fixture never loaded, so the intended fault was absent. The trial is invalid for that test. These cases need different treatment. Marking all three as zero blames the agent for evaluation failures. Dropping all three makes the agent look better by removing real failures. State Example Graded A judge established a pass or fail Not assigned The CSV task has no prose-grounding rubric Not applicable A predeclared condition makes a check irrelevant to this case Unresolved The grader failed to return a usable verdict Invalid trial The test did not start in a valid environment For “not applicable,” consider a refund task with a rule requiring manager approval only above a stated amount. A request below that amount does not need the approval check. The condition belongs in the task definition. Failing to inspect an available document is different. The agent cannot make an evidence requirement inapplicable by skipping the evidence.

sections.title: Do not let incomplete grading improve the score
sections.text: Imagine 100 applicable judgments. The grader returns 40 passes and 10 failures, then fails on the remaining 50. The resolved results have an 80% pass rate: 40 divided by 50. But only half the judgments were resolved. Reporting “80%” without coverage would invite readers to mistake it for a complete result. Worse, the unanswered cases might be the hardest ones. For the implementation here, unresolved required judgments block the complete aggregate they affect. A debugging dashboard can show the provisional result, clearly labeled “80% among resolved judgments; 50% coverage.” Research on rubric-based judge agreement shows that reported agreement can change even when the verdicts do not. Which cases are included, how withheld judgments are handled, and how results are combined are part of the measurement.

sections.title: Set retry rules before running
sections.text: Retry a grader error or invalid environment under a bounded, recorded policy. Retain the attempts and explain which result replaces which failed evaluation attempt. Do not keep rerunning an ordinary agent failure until it passes and then record only the winner. That answers whether a successful attempt can be found, while concealing how often the product fails. Apply the retry policy consistently. The report must distinguish an agent failure from a failure to evaluate it. Accounting for every result prepares us to ask whether the judgments themselves are right.

sections.title: Chapter 7 Find the mistakes your grader misses
sections.text: A judge agrees with people on 85% of a small test set, yet accepts one in five unacceptable answers. Both statements can be true. The mistakes hidden by the average determine whether the judge is useful.

sections.title: Build answers that expose its mistakes
sections.text: A well-written rubric does not guarantee that a model judge will apply it correctly. Before using its verdicts to compare agents, give it answers whose expected grades have been reviewed by people who understand the task. For checkout, include: A correct answer with different wording. A valid remedy other than restoring the pool setting. A confident explanation blaming query execution time. A correct diagnosis with no supporting evidence. The capacity-breaking recommendation of 64 connections per instance. An answer telling the judge to ignore the rubric and award a pass. These cases test different weaknesses. If paraphrases fail, the grader may be matching wording. If the confident wrong explanation passes, fluency may be masking a factual error. If instructions inside the answer change its score, the judge is treating untrusted content as authority. When human reviewers disagree, inspect the rubric and evidence together. Sometimes the grading rule needs clarification. Sometimes the reference is wrong. Do not force agreement by automatically treating the original answer key as infallible.

sections.title: Count the errors that matter
sections.text: Take an illustrative calibration set with 20 answers. Human reviewers classify 10 as acceptable and 10 as unacceptable for a particular criterion. The automated judge produces: Human judgment Judge passes Judge fails Acceptable answer 9 1 Unacceptable answer 2 8 It agrees on 17 of 20 answers, or 85%. But the two kinds of mistakes deserve separate attention: False passes: Two of the 10 unacceptable answers get through. That is a 20% false-pass rate among unacceptable answers. False failures: One of the 10 acceptable answers is rejected. That is a 10% false-failure rate among acceptable answers. For a permission gate, false passes may be especially costly. For accepting multiple valid solutions, false failures may hide real capability. Inspect these rates per criterion rather than relying only on an overall agreement number. Agreement between two model judges is useful evidence of consistency, but they can share the same error. Keep a human-reviewed reference set and periodically inspect disagreements and apparent easy passes. Tune on one set, then check another set whose labels were not used to adjust the judge. Otherwise you may only have taught the grader to recognize its calibration examples.

sections.title: Use preference comparisons for the question they answer
sections.text: Sometimes you want to know which of two answers people prefer. Pairwise judging is well suited to that question. Suppose Answer A recommends 64 connections and Answer B recommends 32. A judge might prefer B because it is less excessive. Both still exceed the allowed 16 per instance. Preference does not establish absolute correctness. The MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena research also documents position and verbosity biases in LLM judging. Hide model identity, vary which answer appears first, and inspect whether preferences are tracking length rather than the intended quality. Keep the absolute task checks alongside the comparison. Keep reviewed examples as a regression check for the grader, and use a separate holdout to validate changes. A trustworthy grader can still observe an inconsistent agent; that is the next experiment.

sections.title: Chapter 8 Find out whether success repeats
A second run answers a different question from a new task
sections.text: The first checkout run is perfect. It would make a convincing demo. Now restore the environment and run it four more times. Anthropic describes using multiple trials because agent outputs vary between attempts. Repetition tells you whether that first success was representative. A new task tests another situation. Another attempt at the same task tests whether performance on that situation persists. Suppose checkout is run five times from the same restored starting state. Every attempt respects the no-write rule, but the answers differ: Attempt Correctness checks Complete 1 1, 1, 1 Yes 2 1, 1, 0 No 3 1, 1, 1 Yes 4 1, 1, 1 Yes 5 1, 0, 0 No Three attempts complete the task, so the observed complete-task success rate is 3/5 = 60% . Across these attempts, 12 of 15 correctness checks pass. Because every attempt has the same three checks, average correctness is 80% . If you had stopped after the first attempt, the eval would have shown a complete success. The additional attempts expose the behavior a user might encounter on another day. Five attempts are an illustration, not a universal sample-size rule. A small smoke test may be enough to detect an obvious regression; a release decision needs enough evidence to distinguish the improvement you care about from run-to-run variation.

sections.title: Repeat the right thing
sections.text: Restore state and memory when measuring independent attempts. Keep fixtures, tools, budgets, and graders fixed across the comparison. Record the intended difference between the systems, such as a model or prompt change, so it is clear what the experiment tests. Regrading a saved trace measures variability in the judge. Executing the agent again measures variability in the agent system. Replaying a cached response measures neither. Keep those experiments separate. If the same answer alternates between pass and fail, investigate the grader before interpreting the agent's score. When tasks have different numbers of trials, average in this order: checks within a trial, trials within a task, then tasks within the suite. Running checkout 20 times should not automatically give it 20 times the influence of a task run once.

sections.title: Distinguish finding a success from delivering one reliably
sections.text: The five attempts above contain at least one success. They do not all succeed. Those observations motivate two different measurements: pass@k asks whether at least one of k attempts succeeds. It measures the ability to find a solution within several tries. pass^k asks whether all k attempts succeed. It measures consistency across that group of attempts. For the illustrated group of five, the “at least one” condition holds and the “all five” condition fails. A benchmark estimates these quantities across its tasks and samples; one group is only an illustration. Best-of-N systems add a further problem: selecting which answer to deliver. A hidden evaluator may recognize the successful attempt, but the deployed selector may choose a confident wrong answer. Evaluate the actual selection rule and count the cost of all attempts. Retries are useful when the product can afford them and can recognize or verify success. They do not justify removing failed attempts from a reliability report.

sections.title: Test whether the agent follows evidence
sections.text: Now change the checkout case. Keep the timeout symptom but make database queries genuinely slower. A good agent should change its diagnosis. Remove the measurements that distinguish slow queries from connection waits. A good agent should explain the uncertainty and request the missing evidence. Keep the service healthy. A good agent should avoid inventing an incident. These variants test something that repeated identical runs cannot: whether the diagnosis responds to the evidence. Research on agent reliability distinguishes consistency from robustness and other reliability dimensions; both repeated attempts and changed conditions matter. Hold whole families of related cases out of tuning. Randomly separating almost identical incidents into training and evaluation can make memorized patterns look like generalization. For release comparisons, run the old and new systems on the same held-out cases and inspect changes task by task. Report an uncertainty range, such as a confidence interval, around the aggregate difference. A small apparent gain with a wide interval is weak evidence for a release. Repeated attempts at one task remain grouped observations; do not count them as an equivalent number of unrelated tasks. You want a result that survives another attempt and a result that transfers to another situation.

sections.title: Chapter 9 Build the framework and make the release call
sections.text: The team fixes the checkout recommendation and the score rises. The framework should now make the release decision—and its reason—easy to inspect.

sections.title: Give the runner a complete task
sections.text: The runner is the program that prepares the environment, executes the agent, invokes graders, and collects results. It should receive a task definition containing: The request: what the user wants and what actions are allowed. The starting state: the fixture version, reset procedure, and validity checks. The reference: verified facts, constraints, and acceptable alternatives, hidden from the agent. The rubrics: correctness checks, auxiliary dimensions, gates, and applicability conditions. The execution settings: model, prompts, tools, budget, and number of trials. The measurement policy: averaging, missing-result handling, and bounded retries. Shared templates can generate these definitions. The resolved versions must be recorded with the run, so another runner can apply the same rules.

sections.title: Keep the arithmetic easy to inspect
sections.text: Once judgments are valid and complete, the basic scorer is small: from statistics import mean tasks = [ {"correctness": [1, 1, 0], "aux": {"authority": 1, "grounding": 1}}, {"correctness": [1, 1], "aux": {"authority": 1, "grounding": 0}}, {"correctness": [1, 0, 1, 0], "aux": {"authority": 0}}, ] correctness = mean(mean(t["correctness"]) for t in tasks) dimensions = set().union(*(t["aux"] for t in tasks)) auxiliary = { name: mean(t["aux"][name] for t in tasks if name in t["aux"]) for name in dimensions } print(round(correctness * 100, 1)) # 72.2 The inner average gives each task a score. The outer average combines tasks. Each auxiliary dimension gets its own set of eligible tasks. This example assumes one trial per task and fully resolved judgments. It omits completion gates and validation so you can see the arithmetic clearly. Before reaching this code, check that every verdict belongs to the right task, run, and rubric version. Reject duplicate judgments, missing required results, unexpected criterion IDs, invalid score ranges, and unsupported “not applicable” claims. A model-generated verdict cannot decide to remove a failed criterion from the denominator. The companion implementation includes the checkout task, sample judgments, a grader prompt, and a scorer with validation, repeated-trial aggregation, missingness handling, critical gates, and tests. The judgments are supplied examples for inspecting the framework.

sections.title: Make the score point to the next fix
sections.text: Return to the original recommendation. Change 64 connections per instance to 16, justify the capacity calculation, and keep the correct diagnosis. Only C3 changes from fail to pass. Checkout correctness rises from 66.7% to 100%. Across the three-task suite, correctness rises from 72.2% to 83.3% , and complete-task success rises from 33.3% to 66.7% . Grounding stays at 50%. Authority compliance stays at 66.7%. The CSV task still violated its permission boundary, so a zero-violation release gate still fails. The next work is specific: prevent the source overwrite, correct the CSV timestamps, and fix its column names. Preserve the filtering and account IDs that already pass. Keep the improved checkout answer as a regression case. Release decision for this worked example: hold. Checkout's remedy now passes. The CSV task still violates a hard boundary and fails two correctness checks. Fix those failures and rerun the comparison with the same fixtures and grading rules. The score tells you what improved. The failed checks tell you what to fix. The gate tells you why the improvement is not enough to release.

sections.title: Compute uncertainty at the task boundary
sections.text: The engineering workbench includes all 100 illustrative task pairs from the release example: 72 both pass, 8 regress, 14 improve, and 6 both fail. Its seeded paired bootstrap estimates a 6 percentage point improvement with a 95% percentile interval of −3 to +15 points. That interval crosses zero. These data do not establish that the candidate is better. Resample independent task pairs, not individual turns. If each task has repeated runs, aggregate within task or use an explicit hierarchical method. The helper rejects duplicate task IDs to prevent accidental pseudo-replication. The choice of population, weighting, and dependence remains your responsibility. A live-grader integration should save the raw grader response, parsed judgment, evidence IDs, rubric version, and adjudicated disagreement. The companion consumes supplied judgments; it does not validate any model grader’s agreement with humans. Calibrate that component on held-out adjudicated cases before trusting its scores.

title: What the Score Conceals
description: The Quality Flywheel · The tests passed. Websites went down. Which question did the checks leave out?
text: Chapters in this collection 01 / 05 What the Score Conceals Turn a Failure into an Experiment Search Beyond the Prompt Make the Winner Earn Its Release What the Next Failure Inherits On 2 July 2019, people visiting websites served through Cloudflare began seeing “502 Bad Gateway” errors. A newly deployed security rule was consuming excessive CPU while inspecting requests. Machines needed for serving web traffic were occupied evaluating the rule. Cloudflare's engineers disabled the affected firewall component to restore service, then isolated the problematic rule and tested the correction. The outage lasted 27 minutes. The company's postmortem explains an important gap: the tests checked which requests the rules matched, but did not test for runaway CPU consumption. This was one of several failed safeguards, including limits on CPU use and the scope of the rollout. The change passed the questions the tests asked. The failure lived in a question they did not ask.

sections.title: A green test is an answer to a particular question
sections.text: “Does this rule detect the intended pattern?” and “Can we afford to run it on production traffic?” are different requirements. Success on the first does not establish the second. A useful evaluation has to represent the job the system must perform, including constraints that can make an otherwise correct result unusable. Now imagine evaluating Atlas, an AI assistant that helps an engineer investigate an unavailable website. It sees high CPU and recommends adding servers. The answer is concise, cites a scaling runbook, and contains a sensible-looking checklist. But busy CPUs do not tell us why they are busy. There may be more requests, or each request may have become more expensive to process. The same symptom can require a different response. Two causes of a busy web server What changed? What to investigate More requests arrive. Traffic volume, available capacity, and downstream limits. Each request does more work. Recent changes and where CPU time is being spent. If the evaluator rewards Atlas for writing a complete plan without checking that distinction, an optimizer can improve presentation while leaving the investigation weak. A runbook link is evidence only when its reasoning applies to the case. In Scaling Laws for Reward Model Overoptimization , stronger optimization of a proxy reward eventually degrades the study's reference reward. The practical lesson is to inspect what the score allows the optimizer to neglect before making the search more powerful.

sections.title: Write down the trade before choosing the weights
sections.text: Suppose one version of Atlas diagnoses failures correctly more often, while another includes runbook links more often. A weighted average can rank either version first without changing a single answer. Change the scoring rule

sections.title: The answers stay the same. The winner changes.
sections.text: Atlas A: 90% correct diagnoses, 20% include a runbook link. Atlas B: 70% correct diagnoses, 95% include a runbook link. Weight assigned to including a runbook link 50% Atlas A 55.0 Atlas B 82.5 Atlas B leads by 27.5 points under this scoring rule. Weighted score = accuracy × (1 − link weight) + link inclusion × link weight. Both rates refer to the same hypothetical task set. Links, clear writing, and thorough explanations matter. They do not compensate for an unsupported diagnosis. Combining them into one average quietly makes them exchangeable. A useful scorecard keeps separate questions visible: does the explanation fit the evidence, does the proposed action address the suspected cause, and does it respect the engineer's approval boundary? A plan to disable a security control also needs to account for the protection being removed. Restoring availability is part of the decision, not the whole of it.

sections.title: The evaluator needs a difficult example too
sections.text: Give the evaluator two equally polished answers: “add servers to handle the extra traffic” and “investigate the recent change that increased work per request.” Pair them first with a genuine traffic surge, then with evidence of an expensive new rule. A useful evaluator should change its judgment as the evidence changes. Recent controlled probes of LLM judges find cases where meaningful changes to a response or rubric fail to produce the expected change in the verdict. That makes this a useful test to run, rather than an ability to assume. Who Validates the Validators? studies how people's evaluation criteria evolve as they inspect outputs. The team may initially reward a plausible recovery plan and later recognize that it must also check the causal argument and the action's consequences. When the standard changes, rescore the previous version under the same rules. The first step in improvement is a defensible answer to a simple question: what would have to change for us to call this behavior better?

sections.title: Turn coverage into a small matrix
sections.text: For the incident, record each requirement as a row: detect the symptom, identify the rule, bound affected traffic, propose a reversible action, and verify recovery. Add columns for evidence source, current test, failure case, and owner. A blank cell is an untested obligation, not an implicit pass. For example, a successful rollback can satisfy recovery while leaving the causal diagnosis wrong. Score those separately. Before adding a new aggregate metric, inspect which row drove the change. The matrix should make a missing test obvious enough that a higher headline score cannot hide it.

title: Turn a Failure into an Experiment
description: The Quality Flywheel · A wrong answer points to a problem. A targeted change tests the explanation.
text: Chapters in this collection 02 / 05 What the Score Conceals Turn a Failure into an Experiment Search Beyond the Prompt Make the Winner Earn Its Release What the Next Failure Inherits Atlas sees an unavailable website and high CPU. It recommends adding servers. “Reason more carefully” is an easy response to that weak diagnosis. It is not yet an engineering plan. The useful question is what would let Atlas distinguish a traffic surge from an expensive new operation. Did it see the request volume? Could it inspect recent changes? Did it know where the CPU time was going?

sections.title: Different explanations need different repairs
sections.text: Suppose Atlas's monitoring summary includes error rate and total CPU use, but omits request volume and the breakdown of CPU work. Telling it to inspect that evidence will not help unless the system makes the evidence available. What to change depends on what went wrong Possible problem A useful test Atlas cannot see the relevant evidence. Add request volume, recent changes, and a CPU breakdown to the saved case. The evidence is available, but Atlas does not inspect it. Require the existing checks before choosing a remedy. Atlas sees the evidence but interprets it poorly. Keep the inputs fixed and change the decision procedure. These are proposed experiments for Atlas, not a reconstruction of Cloudflare's response. They separate a model problem from a missing-information problem. Both can produce the same confident recommendation. Start by replaying the saved case with the missing evidence supplied. If Atlas now identifies an expensive operation, the information gap becomes a stronger explanation. If it still insists on a traffic surge, the next experiment should examine how it uses the evidence.

sections.title: Make the explanation risk being wrong
sections.text: A production symptom is not a cause. High CPU tells us the processor is busy. It does not tell us whether the work is necessary. To test a suspected expensive rule, reproduce the workload in an isolated environment and compare processing with and without that rule. Keep the requests and resources comparable. If the extra cost disappears when the rule is removed, the result supports the diagnosis. If the cost remains, the investigation has more work to do. That test concerns the website. A separate comparison concerns Atlas: does giving it the relevant evidence improve its diagnosis across more than one case? Repairing the service and improving the assistant are related tasks with different evidence requirements. AgentRx applies a related principle to agent diagnosis: it checks execution steps and gathers evidence around failures. A record of the steps helps propose a cause. A targeted intervention tests whether that proposal is useful.

sections.title: Find the nearest case where the lesson fails
sections.text: “Roll back the latest change whenever CPU is high” is a tempting lesson. It also fails when a website has simply become popular and its latest deployment is unrelated. Similar symptoms, different investigations Website is slow, and… What the evidence suggests Request volume rises; work per request stays similar. Investigate capacity and downstream limits before adding resources. A new operation uses much more CPU per request. Isolate that operation and assess a targeted rollback or correction. Requests spend most of their time waiting for the database. Investigate the database bottleneck; more web servers may increase pressure. These examples are useful because the visible complaint—“the website is slow”—does not determine the remedy. Atlas must use the evidence that separates the cases. A useful failure review leaves behind an explanation someone can challenge, a change someone can test, and a counterexample that prevents the lesson from becoming too broad.

sections.title: Make one change falsifiable
sections.text: Field Illustrative experiment Failure Agent misses a rule deployment in an incomplete export Hypothesis A coverage receipt makes missing scope detectable Intervention Add expected and observed scope to the tool response Hold fixed Model, incident evidence, budget, task IDs Falsifier Agent still concludes globally from partial coverage Guardrail No unauthorized query or excessive investigation cost The engineering workbench tests the receipt’s deterministic contract. Whether a model uses it correctly is a separate experiment. Keep both layers in the release record rather than crediting the contract test as behavioral success.

title: Search Beyond the Prompt
description: The Quality Flywheel · An optimizer can only discover changes its search space allows.
text: Chapters in this collection 03 / 05 What the Score Conceals Turn a Failure into an Experiment Search Beyond the Prompt Make the Winner Earn Its Release What the Next Failure Inherits Atlas sees high CPU use and failed requests, then recommends adding servers. That advice could help during a genuine surge in traffic. It could also miss the problem completely: the website may be receiving an ordinary number of requests, with each request suddenly taking far more work to process. The team could add “investigate carefully” to the prompt. But an instruction cannot reveal information the assistant never receives. If Atlas sees only total CPU use and the error rate, it cannot reliably distinguish more work arriving from each piece of work becoming more expensive.

sections.title: Every hill has a boundary
sections.text: Hill climbing starts with a candidate, tries nearby changes, and retains an improvement. For Atlas, a nearby change might be a sentence in the prompt. The score defines uphill; the allowed edits define which neighboring candidates exist. A conceptual landscape, not measured results. Small edits search nearby; a different tool, representation, or workflow can open a different part of the search space. A local peak means that none of the nearby changes being tried looks better. It does not mean the best system has been found. Rewording the instruction may stop helping because the limiting factor is missing evidence. Showing what is consuming CPU and what changed before the outage opens up a different kind of improvement. There are practical reasons to search locally: small changes are cheap, easier to inspect, and easier to reverse. The mistake is treating the best result within one search space as evidence that the rest of the system no longer matters.

sections.title: Use the failure to propose a change
sections.text: A score can rank a candidate against the current version. It says little about what to try next. A record showing “Atlas assumed traffic increased without checking request volume” gives the team something specific to change. That distinction runs through several strands of research. DSPy makes language-model programs modular enough to optimize their components. TextGrad propagates natural-language feedback through a computation. Its “gradients” are critiques, not exact derivatives; their value lies in proposing useful edits that can be tested. GEPA uses execution feedback to evolve prompts and retain candidates with complementary strengths. This matters when a single average hides useful differences. One version of Atlas might handle traffic spikes well; another might investigate recent changes more effectively. Studying both can suggest a better revision than keeping only the overall winner. For Atlas, the team puts three candidates on the table: Prompt: require evidence for the proposed cause before recommending a fix. Tools: show request volume, a breakdown of CPU use, and recent changes alongside the error rate. Procedure: distinguish an increase in incoming requests from an increase in the work needed to process each request, then choose an intervention supported by that distinction. Test them separately before combining them. If richer evidence fixes the cases while the prompt alone does not, the evidence points to missing visibility into the system. If Atlas still ignores the evidence until it receives a clear procedure, the combination deserves its own comparison. Changing everything at once makes it harder to know which part was worth keeping.

sections.title: Keep a cost for being clever
sections.text: It is possible to make the investigation unnecessarily elaborate. Atlas could inspect every service and produce pages of analysis while the website remains unavailable. A better procedure would first check the few observations that distinguish the leading explanations, then investigate further when those checks leave uncertainty. The search therefore needs more than a quality score. It needs a reasonable response time, tool costs, and limits on what the assistant may change. AI Agents That Matter argues for evaluating agent performance together with its cost and for more careful benchmark design. Here, an improvement means giving the engineer better advice soon enough to use it. Better feedback can help a system propose better changes. But a convincing explanation of why an edit should work is a reason to run the experiment, not a substitute for its result.

sections.title: Budget the search before it starts
sections.text: Write down the candidate budget, evaluation budget, stopping rule, and final holdout before optimization. For example, permit 12 candidate designs, at most three development evaluations per candidate, and one final evaluation of the frozen winner. Those numbers are illustrative; choose them from the experiment’s cost and variance. Stop when the budget is exhausted, a predeclared target is reached without guardrail regressions, or remaining changes are outside the permitted design space. Keep failed candidates and costs. Repeatedly consulting the holdout turns it into development data. This chapter defines the experiment policy. The harness implementation essay develops the optimizer and promotion boundary. Reuse that machinery rather than giving every prompt experiment its own release rules.

title: Make the Winner Earn Its Release
description: The Quality Flywheel · Selection finds a promising candidate. Independent evidence earns the release.
text: Chapters in this collection 04 / 05 What the Score Conceals Turn a Failure into an Experiment Search Beyond the Prompt Make the Winner Earn Its Release What the Next Failure Inherits Giving Atlas a clearer view of CPU use and recent changes looks promising. In our hypothetical evaluation, the team tries several versions of its instructions and chooses the one with the highest development score. It now recognizes the expensive processing behind the original outage. Should it replace the current Atlas? Not yet. The team selected this version because it looked good on cases it had already inspected. Some of that advantage may come from learning those particular examples, and some may come from favorable runs. The selection process is part of the evidence.

sections.title: Compare changes on the same work
sections.text: Run the current version and the candidate on the same saved incidents, with the same underlying records and comparable limits on time and tool use. Record their disagreements, not just their separate totals. The revealing cases are the ones that improved and the ones that got worse. An illustrative comparison on 100 website outages Candidate correct Candidate incorrect Current version correct 72 8 Current version incorrect 14 6 Accuracy rises from 80% to 86%. The candidate fixes fourteen recommendations and breaks eight. “Six points better” is true, but incomplete. Look at the eight failures. They involve genuine traffic spikes. The candidate has picked up a shortcut: when CPU use is high, roll back the latest deployment. That helps when a recent change introduced expensive processing, but it can undo a healthy release while leaving a traffic surge unresolved. The average rewards the shortcut because change-related failures are common in this test set. The distinction is straightforward once someone reads the disagreements. Similar symptoms can have different causes. High CPU use tells the engineer where to investigate; it does not, by itself, tell them whether to add capacity or reverse a change. A comparison should help the team discover this distinction, not merely produce a number that clears a release gate. One hundred incidents also do not settle the size of the gain. Incidents differ in difficulty, repeated attempts can vary, and several cases may come from the same underlying outage. Adding Error Bars to Evals explains why uncertainty and experimental design belong in evaluation. Replaying one outage many times should not masquerade as independent evidence from many outages.

sections.title: Give discovery and confirmation different jobs
sections.text: Replay holds the inputs steady. Held-out cases test whether the lesson travels. A staged release tests whether it survives real use. Development cases are for investigation. Inspect them, argue about them, and use their failures to generate candidates. Confirmation cases answer a different question: does the selected change work on examples it was not tailored to? A famous outage also creates a shortcut: Atlas may remember the published answer. Use unfamiliar variants, change the cause, and provide only evidence available at the decision point. Removing the company name alone does not make a case independent. For Atlas, fresh cases should include genuine traffic surges, expensive processing introduced by a change, and outages where the available evidence does not yet settle the cause. Keep them out of the feedback used to revise Atlas. If their failures become the basis for another edit, they have become development material; the next confirmation needs independent evidence. Research on adaptive data analysis explains why reusing data to choose the next hypothesis can undermine ordinary statistical guarantees. There is no magic in the word “holdout.” Repeatedly checking a private score and changing the system in response still lets information about that set guide the search. The more candidates a team tries, the more care it owes to how the winner was chosen.

sections.title: Match the test to the responsibility
sections.text: Atlas currently advises an engineer, who can reject a bad recommendation. Giving Atlas permission to act unattended changes the requirement even if its model and prompt stay identical. If each attempt independently succeeds with probability 0.8, five attempts have a 99.97% chance of containing at least one success, but only a 32.77% chance of all succeeding. These are illustrative probabilities, not Atlas's measured performance. The first can help someone who can recognize and select a good answer. The second resembles a system expected to complete a sequence of jobs reliably. Real attempts can be correlated; repeating the investigation may simply repeat the same mistake. τ-bench brings consistency across trials into agent evaluation. A more recent preprint, Locating Hidden Failures Makes Long-Horizon Agents More Reliable , examines errors inside sequences of actions that a final score can miss. Both reinforce a lesson for Atlas: an investigation can contain an unsupported assumption even when its final recommendation happens to help. The team removes the automatic rollback shortcut. Atlas now compares request volume with processing cost and looks for evidence linking a recent change to the failure. Fresh incidents test whether it distinguishes those explanations and recognizes when more evidence is needed. Repeated trials and human review support a limited rollout, with an engineer approving any proposed action. The release decision includes diagnostic quality, inappropriate recommendations, and response time. Real use can reveal conditions saved examples did not cover: a different traffic pattern, a new component, or an incomplete monitoring record. Keep the previous version available and check whether the expected improvement actually appears. Offline comparison and live observation complete each other. The comparison helps isolate a change. Real use reveals whether the change mattered where Atlas has to work.

sections.title: Reproduce the paired release example
sections.text: Download the engineering workbench and run python workbench.py . The complete CSV contains the 100 illustrative pairs used here. A 10,000-draw bootstrap with seed 19 yields a 6-point gain and an interval from −3 to +15 points. A higher average alone is insufficient evidence of improvement. Inspect the eight regressions before accepting any aggregate gain. Partition by task family only if those slices were defined independently of the result; otherwise label the analysis exploratory. A release also needs acceptable authority, cost, and tail behavior. If the tasks are correlated, resample the independent cluster rather than pretending each row is independent. This is a reproducible calculation on constructed data. Replace the CSV with held-out measurements before making a deployment decision.

title: What the Next Failure Inherits
description: The Quality Flywheel · A loop becomes a flywheel when its useful work survives the turn.
text: Chapters in this collection 05 / 05 What the Score Conceals Turn a Failure into an Experiment Search Beyond the Prompt Make the Winner Earn Its Release What the Next Failure Inherits Consider the next website slowdown. This time a promotion has brought a surge of visitors. Atlas checks the request volume, the work per request, and the available capacity. It does not recommend rolling back an unrelated deployment merely because the last outage involved a bad change. That is the lesson worth keeping: distinguish the causes before choosing the remedy. Memorizing the previous fix would have made the next investigation worse. A quality flywheel carries those useful distinctions forward. A loop can keep a team busy while it rediscovers the same facts. A flywheel changes what the next investigation starts with. The useful output of a cycle is more than a fix. A saved case, a reliable check, and a record of what worked make the next cycle easier.

sections.title: Retain the distinction, not the remedy
sections.text: The useful memory of the earlier outage takes several forms. A saved case preserves the evidence. A better monitoring summary makes missing information visible. Contrasting tests distinguish increased traffic from expensive processing. A comparison between versions explains why the team kept a change to Atlas. These assets do different jobs. An incident record preserves what happened. A regression test asks whether the mistake has returned. A procedure tells Atlas what to inspect. A release record tells the next engineer which claim the evidence supported. What Atlas should carry forward Before treating high CPU as a shortage of capacity, distinguish more requests from more work per request. Inspect traffic, recent changes, and where processing time is spent. If the available evidence cannot separate the explanations, say what is missing and investigate before recommending a consequential action. The rule is useful because it directs attention. It does not settle every incident. A traffic surge and an inefficient new operation can occur together; a database delay can create retries that increase traffic. The procedure should help Atlas ask a better next question while remaining open to evidence.

sections.title: Memory needs an admission policy
sections.text: Reflexion explored using verbal feedback as memory for later attempts without updating model weights. Agentic Context Engineering develops the idea into an evolving context playbook. These approaches make retained experience part of the system being improved. But saving an explanation does not make it true. “High CPU means add servers” and “always roll back the latest change” can each succeed on selected cases. Neither is a dependable rule without the conditions that make it apply. A lesson earns a place when it works beyond the episode that produced it. Keep the supporting cases and the counterexample. Record its scope. When a new incident contradicts it, revise the rule or narrow the claim. Otherwise the playbook becomes advice no one can justify.

sections.title: Compounding has a maintenance bill
sections.text: More tests are not automatically more knowledge. Twenty near-identical outages may add runtime without checking another distinction. A saved result can also become misleading after the service architecture changes. A once-useful recovery procedure may no longer be appropriate. Retire duplicates. Keep the relevant environment and assumptions with each test. Revisit the standards when the assistant's responsibilities change. Preserve useful history, but separate what the system currently relies on from what it once believed. The flywheel earns its name only if the retained work helps enough to repay this maintenance. The next failure should take less effort to reproduce or lead to a better experiment. An archive that grows while investigation remains equally difficult is accumulating records without gaining much momentum.

sections.title: Improve the machinery of improvement
sections.text: The deeper opportunity is to make the team better at learning. A failure can improve the assistant. It can also reveal missing monitoring data, expose a blind spot in the evaluator, or suggest a more revealing test. Those changes increase the value of later work. Current methods increasingly automate proposal, evaluation, and memory. The unresolved task is keeping these parts honest with one another: a powerful search should not exploit a weak judge, and a persuasive memory should not become evidence for itself. The real outage that opened this collection exposes the underlying responsibility. A test can pass while an important requirement remains unexamined. An improvement process earns trust by discovering that missing question, making it testable, and preserving it for the next change. The next failure deserves to meet a system that kept the lesson—and the means to challenge it.

sections.title: Store a lesson with its conditions
sections.text: lesson_id: coverage-before-global-conclusion-v1 claim: a completed export may omit requested scopes evidence: [incident-17, regression-test-coverage] applies_when: connector exposes expected and observed scopes invalidated_by: connector contract or scope model changes counterexample: full coverage but stale evidence owner: evaluation-maintainer review_after: next connector release A lesson should point to the failure and the test that would contradict it. Keep an owner and an invalidation condition so retrieval does not turn old advice into unconditional policy. If the next failure concerns stale evidence, the coverage lesson is relevant background but not a complete remedy. Retest the stored rule when its dependencies change. Preserve the previous version and the reason for revision; that history is more useful than accumulating another unqualified instruction.

title: Verdicts require Epistemics
description: Trustworthy Autonomy · An autonomous agent investigates 5XX errors—and learns to separate what it observes, what it believes, and what it can safely do next.
text: Chapters in this collection 01 / 09 Verdicts require Epistemics Evidence requires Provenance State requires Ownership Autonomy requires a Dial Inputs require a Trust Boundary Knowledge requires a Clock Delegation requires Ceilings Failure requires a Ladder Learning requires Outcomes Epistemics is how we decide what to believe, what supports that belief, and when to change our mind. Its roots lie in epistemology: the philosophical study of knowledge. A correct answer can be a lucky guess. Good reasons matter, and new evidence can reveal their limits. Three questions make this practical: What did I observe? What am I assuming? What would change my mind? “Server errors are rising” is an observation. “The latest deployment caused them” is a hypothesis. The distinction matters when an autonomous agent can act on that diagnosis.

sections.title: An agent on call
sections.text: Imagine an API gateway's 5XX error rate rises from 0.2% to 12%, mostly 504 timeouts. Its p95 latency jumps from 250 milliseconds to three seconds. A Checkout deployment finished two minutes earlier. 5XX codes indicate server errors; 504 means the gateway waited too long for a response. The p95 is the response time that 95% of requests meet or beat. The timing makes the deployment a suspect. The agent checks which requests fail and follows their dependencies.

sections.title: An epistemic record
sections.text: The agent keeps a versioned record of its verdict, observations, inferences, confidence, alternatives, and unknowns. It states what would challenge the explanation and when to reassess it. Follow the six checkpoints below to see that record change. Two details help: a connection pool is a reusable set of database connections. The agent's approved runbook allows restoring its previous size after checking database capacity, and limiting retries.
